battle:diu-1509.text: February 1509, off the coast of Gujarat. A combined fleet of the Mamluks of Egypt, the Sultan of Gujarat and the ruler of Calicut, quietly backed by Venice, sets out to drive the Portuguese newcomers from the spice trade. Francisco de Almeida's ships are armed with heavy cannon, and they shatter it. It is often called the moment European naval power arrived in Asia, and it opens a century of Portuguese dominance over Asian sea trade.

battle:chaldiran.text: August 1514, in the highlands of eastern Anatolia. The Ottoman Sultan Selim the First faces Shah Ismail of Persia, whose famous horsemen have never lost a battle. But Selim has artillery, and Janissaries armed with muskets, and the Persian cavalry breaks against them. The line drawn here between the Ottoman and Persian worlds still lies close to today's border between Turkey and Iran, and it hardened the divide between Sunni and Shia.

battle:marj-dabiq.text: August 1516, near Aleppo, in Syria. Selim's guns destroy the army of the Mamluk Sultanate, and its old sultan, Qansuh al-Ghawri, dies on the field. Within months Cairo has fallen, ending a dynasty of slave-soldiers that had ruled Egypt for more than 250 years. The Ottoman Empire doubles in size, and its sultan becomes the guardian of Mecca and Medina.

battle:tenochtitlan:0.text: This is the fall of Tenochtitlan, in 1521. Tenochtitlan is the capital of the Aztec Empire, a city of perhaps 200,000 people, built on an island in a lake, in the Valley of Mexico. In red is the Aztec Empire. In blue are a few hundred Spanish soldiers, under Hernán Cortés, and tens of thousands of their native allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, old enemies of the Aztecs.

battle:tenochtitlan:1.text: Cortés had first reached the city in 1519, from the coast at Veracruz. Follow the blue arrow inland. The emperor, Moctezuma, received him, and was taken prisoner. In 1520, Moctezuma died, and the Spaniards were driven out of the city in a bloody night of fighting. Then smallpox, brought from Europe, swept through Tenochtitlan, killing great numbers, among them the new emperor.

battle:tenochtitlan:2.text: In May 1521, Cortés returns with his allies, and lays siege to the city, with boats built to fight on the lake. For 93 days, the Aztecs, led by their young emperor, Cuauhtémoc, fight street by street. On the 13th of August, the city falls. It is razed, and Mexico City is built on its ruins. Three centuries of Spanish rule in Mexico begin, won as much by native allies as by Spanish steel.

battle:pavia.text: February 1525, in a walled hunting park near Pavia, in northern Italy. The French knights of King Francis the First charge, and Spanish arquebusiers cut them down. Francis himself is captured, and carried off to Madrid. The battle makes the Emperor Charles the Fifth master of Italy, and marks the turning point from armoured cavalry to firearms.

battle:panipat-1:0.text: This is the First Battle of Panipat, fought on the 21st of April 1526, on the plain north of Delhi. In red is the Delhi Sultanate, ruled by Ibrahim Lodi, with a large army and many war elephants. In blue is a much smaller army from Kabul, led by Babur, a prince descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, who has lost his homeland in Central Asia, and now looks to India.

battle:panipat-1:1.text: Follow the blue arrow down from Kabul. Babur brings something new to India: field guns, and soldiers with matchlock muskets. At Panipat, he lashes some 700 carts together as a barrier, with gaps for his cannon and his horsemen. When Lodi's army attacks, Babur's cavalry sweeps around its flanks, and the noise of the guns panics the war elephants.

battle:panipat-1:2.text: Within hours, the battle is over, and Ibrahim Lodi lies dead on the field. Babur takes Delhi and Agra, and the Delhi Sultanate comes to an end. Here begins the Mughal Empire, which will build the Taj Mahal, and shape the history of South Asia for more than 300 years.

battle:mohacs:0.text: This is the Battle of Mohács, fought on the 29th of August 1526, in southern Hungary. The Ottoman Empire is at the height of its power, under Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. In blue is his army, far larger than its enemy, with many guns. In red is the Kingdom of Hungary, under its young king, Louis the Second, with about 25,000 men.

battle:mohacs:1.text: Follow the blue arrow from Constantinople. Suleiman marches up the Danube, through the Balkans. The Hungarians, outnumbered, meet him on a marshy plain near Mohács. Their heavy cavalry charges, and breaks into the Ottoman lines, but is caught by the Ottoman guns and Janissaries. In less than two hours, the Hungarian army is destroyed.

battle:mohacs:2.text: King Louis flees, and drowns in a stream, still in his armour. He leaves no heir. Hungary is split for 150 years: the Ottomans take the centre, Transylvania becomes their vassal, and the Habsburgs claim the rest, with the Hungarian crown. The Ottomans now stand at the gates of central Europe, and three years later, they besiege Vienna for the first time.

battle:cajamarca:0.text: This is the Battle of Cajamarca, on the 16th of November 1532, in the Andes. The Inca Empire is the largest state in the Americas, stretching along the mountains for thousands of kilometres. It has just come through a civil war, and smallpox has already swept through it. In red is the Inca Empire, under its new emperor, Atahualpa. In blue is a small Spanish force, of fewer than 200 men, under Francisco Pizarro.

battle:cajamarca:1.text: Follow the blue arrow up from the coast. Pizarro reaches the town of Cajamarca, where Atahualpa is camped with an army of many thousands. Pizarro invites him to a meeting in the town square. Atahualpa arrives, carried on a litter, with thousands of unarmed attendants. At a signal, the Spaniards open fire with guns and cannon, and charge with their horses. In the panic, thousands are killed, and Atahualpa is taken prisoner.

battle:cajamarca:2.text: To win his freedom, Atahualpa offers to fill a room with gold, and twice over with silver. The ransom is paid, but in 1533 the Spaniards kill him anyway. With its emperor gone, the empire falls apart, and Pizarro marches on Cusco. The gold and silver of the Andes will help pay for Spain's wars in Europe for a century.

battle:panipat-2.text: November 1556, on the same plain of Panipat. Hemu, who has taken Delhi, is winning the battle when an arrow strikes him in the eye. His army breaks. On the other side is the Mughal heir, a boy of just 13 named Akbar. Mughal rule is saved at its most fragile moment, and Akbar will reign for nearly fifty years, as the greatest of the Mughals.

battle:talikota.text: January 1565, in the Deccan of southern India. Four rival sultanates unite against the greatest power in the south, the Vijayanagara Empire. Its regent, Rama Raya, is captured and beheaded, and the magnificent city of Vijayanagara is sacked for months. Its ruins, at Hampi, are now a World Heritage Site, and the south is opened to new powers.

battle:malta-1565.text: May 1565. A great Ottoman fleet and some 35,000 men land on the island of Malta. Against them stand the Knights Hospitaller under their grand master, Jean de Valette, with Maltese soldiers, about 6,000 in all. For nearly four months they hold their forts under one of the heaviest bombardments of the age. When a small relief force finally lands, the Ottomans sail away. Malta's capital, Valletta, built afterwards, is named after the grand master.

battle:lepanto:0.text: This is the Battle of Lepanto, fought on the 7th of October 1571, in the Gulf of Patras, off western Greece. The Ottoman Empire is the great power of the Mediterranean, and is taking Cyprus from Venice. In red is the Ottoman fleet, under Ali Pasha. In blue is the Holy League, an alliance of Spain, Venice, the Pope and other Catholic states, under the young Don John of Austria.

battle:lepanto:1.text: Follow the blue arrow from Sicily. The two fleets meet at the mouth of the gulf, some 450 ships in all, in the largest battle of galleys in history. Galleys are rowed by hundreds of oarsmen, many of them slaves, and they fight like armies at sea, ramming and boarding at point-blank range. The Holy League's six great galleasses, floating gun platforms, break up the Ottoman line.

battle:lepanto:2.text: In a few hours, the Ottoman fleet is all but destroyed, and Ali Pasha is killed. Thousands of Christian galley slaves are set free. Among the wounded on the League's side is a Spanish soldier, Miguel de Cervantes, who loses the use of his left hand, and will later write Don Quixote. Europe celebrates, but within a year, the Ottomans have built a new fleet.

battle:alcacer-quibir.text: August 1578, in northern Morocco. Portugal's young King Sebastian leads a crusade into Morocco, and his army is annihilated. Sebastian vanishes in the battle, with no heir, and two rival Moroccan sultans die too. Two years later, Philip the Second of Spain claims the Portuguese throne, and for decades, impostors appear claiming to be the lost king.

battle:armada:0.text: This is the story of the Spanish Armada, in the summer of 1588. King Philip the Second of Spain rules the greatest empire in the world. In red is Spain, Catholic, and angered by England's support for the Dutch rebels, and by English raids on its treasure ships. In blue is Protestant England, under Queen Elizabeth the First. Philip plans to invade it.

battle:armada:1.text: A fleet of about 130 ships sails from Spain. Follow the red arrow north. It is to sail up the Channel, and meet a Spanish army in the Netherlands, to carry it across to England. The English ships, smaller, faster, and armed with long-range guns, harry it all the way up the Channel. Then, off Calais, at night, the English send in fireships, and the Armada's tight formation breaks.

battle:armada:2.text: The next day, off Gravelines, the English attack the scattered fleet. A shifting wind drives the Armada north, into the North Sea, and with no way back, it sails for home around Scotland and Ireland. Follow the red arrow north. Autumn gales wreck dozens of ships on the Irish coast. About 50 of the 130 ships are lost. Protestant England is safe, and Elizabeth's reign enters legend.

battle:imjin-war:0.text: This is the Imjin War, fought in Korea from 1592 to 1598. In red is Japan, newly united under the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi. In blue are Joseon Korea and its great neighbour, Ming China, which sends armies to help. Hideyoshi's real target is China itself, and Korea lies in the way. Watch the map: the red arrow crosses the narrow strait from Japan to the port of Busan.

battle:imjin-war:1.text: In May 1592, a huge Japanese army lands at Busan. Its soldiers carry muskets, which Korea's troops have rarely faced. Within three weeks they take the capital, Seoul, and the king flees north. By summer they reach Pyongyang. Follow the red arrow up the peninsula.

battle:imjin-war:2.text: But at sea, Korea has Admiral Yi Sun-sin. His fleet, with its armoured turtle ships, wins battle after battle, and cuts the Japanese supply lines. On land, Korean guerrillas rise in every province. In early 1593, a Ming army crosses the Yalu River and retakes Pyongyang. Watch the blue arrow come down from China. The Japanese fall back to the southern coast, and years of talks begin.

battle:imjin-war:3.text: In 1597, the talks fail, and Japan invades again. Admiral Yi, briefly dismissed, returns, and at Myeongnyang he defeats a far larger fleet with just 13 ships. In 1598, Hideyoshi dies, and the Japanese armies sail home. Yi falls in the war's last sea battle, at Noryang. Perhaps a million people have died. Korea is left devastated, the Ming are weakened, and in Japan, the Tokugawa rise to power.

battle:sekigahara:0.text: This is the Battle of Sekigahara, fought on the 21st of October 1600, in central Japan. For more than a century, Japan has been torn by civil war between rival lords. The great unifier, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, has died, leaving a young son. In blue is the Eastern Army of Tokugawa Ieyasu, the most powerful lord in Japan. Against it stands the Western Army, led by Ishida Mitsunari, loyal to the Toyotomi.

battle:sekigahara:1.text: Follow the arrows: the two armies march to meet in a narrow mountain valley at Sekigahara, on the main road between east and west. Together, they number more than 150,000 men. The battle begins in thick morning fog. For hours, it is evenly balanced. On a hill above the field waits Kobayakawa Hideaki, with 15,000 men of the Western Army, who has secretly promised to change sides.

battle:sekigahara:2.text: At midday, Kobayakawa's troops attack their own allies, and others follow. The Western Army collapses within hours. Ishida Mitsunari is captured, and executed. Three years later, Ieyasu becomes shogun. The Tokugawa shogunate will rule Japan for more than 250 years, a long age of peace, and of isolation from the world.

battle:thirty-years:0.text: This is the Thirty Years' War, fought from 1618 to 1648 across the German lands of the Holy Roman Empire. In red are the Holy Roman Emperor, of the Habsburg family, and his Spanish cousins. In blue are the Protestant princes, and later Denmark, Sweden and France. It begins as a quarrel over religion, Catholic against Protestant, and becomes a struggle for mastery of Europe.

battle:thirty-years:1.text: In May 1618, in Prague, Protestant nobles of Bohemia throw the emperor's officials out of a castle window. The men survive the fall, but the rebellion has begun. The Bohemians choose a Protestant king, Frederick of the Palatinate. In 1620, at the Battle of White Mountain, just outside Prague, the emperor's armies crush them. Follow the red arrow north from Vienna.

battle:thirty-years:2.text: Denmark joins the war, and is beaten. Then, in 1630, the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus lands on the Baltic coast with a modern, disciplined army. Follow the blue arrow south from Sweden. He wins great victories, but falls in battle at Lützen in 1632. Catholic France, fearing the Habsburgs more than the Protestants, then joins the war against them. Armies live off the land, and plague and famine follow them.

battle:thirty-years:3.text: In 1648, after years of talks, the Peace of Westphalia ends the war. The cost is terrible. Somewhere between 4.5 and 8 million people are dead, and some regions of Germany lose a third of their people, or more. The emperor's power is broken, France rises as Europe's leading power, and the Netherlands and Switzerland are recognised as independent. The peace is often seen as the birth of the modern idea of sovereign states.

battle:shanhai-pass.text: May 1644. Rebels have just taken Beijing, and the last Ming emperor has hanged himself. At Shanhai Pass, where the Great Wall meets the sea, General Wu Sangui makes a fateful choice. He opens the gate to the Manchus, and together they break the rebel army. The Qing move into Beijing, and will rule China until 1912.

battle:naseby.text: June 1645, in the fields of Northamptonshire. Parliament's New Model Army, disciplined and professional, under Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell, destroys King Charles the First's last main army. Four years later, the king is executed, and England becomes, for a time, a republic. Royal power in Britain will never again be what it was.

battle:mughal-maratha:0.text: This is the long war between the Mughal Empire and the Marathas, fought from 1681 to 1707 across the Deccan, the high plateau of western and southern India. In red is the Mughal Empire, under the emperor Aurangzeb, the largest and richest state in India. In blue is the Maratha kingdom, founded in the hills of the western Deccan by Shivaji, who died in 1680. Watch the map: this war is fought among hills, valleys and great stone forts.

battle:mughal-maratha:1.text: In 1681, Aurangzeb leaves Delhi and moves his whole court south. He means to crush the Marathas, and to conquer the last independent kingdoms of the Deccan. Follow the red arrow down from Delhi. He takes Bijapur and Golconda, and in 1689 his men capture Shivaji's son, the Maratha king Sambhaji, who is put to death.

battle:mughal-maratha:2.text: But the Marathas do not give in. Sambhaji's brother, Rajaram, carries on the fight from the fortress of Jinji, far to the south. When Rajaram dies in 1700, his widow, Tarabai, leads the resistance. Maratha horsemen raid deep into Mughal lands, while the emperor's huge armies spend years besieging one hill fort after another.

battle:mughal-maratha:3.text: In 1707, Aurangzeb dies in the Deccan, aged 88, never having gone home. The war has drained his treasury and his armies. After his death, Mughal power declines quickly, and the Marathas spread north, to become the leading power in India in the 18th century. The long campaign that was meant to end the Marathas had made them stronger.

battle:vienna-1683:0.text: This is the Battle of Vienna, fought on the 12th of September 1683. The Ottoman Empire is at the height of its power in Europe, and holds most of Hungary. In red is a huge Ottoman army, under the Grand Vizier, Kara Mustafa Pasha. Follow the red arrow north from Constantinople. In blue are the Habsburg Emperor, the German princes, and the King of Poland, John the Third Sobieski.

battle:vienna-1683:1.text: In July, the Ottomans surround Vienna, and lay siege to it. For two months, the city's small garrison holds out, while Ottoman miners dig tunnels to blow up its walls. Disease and hunger spread inside. By early September, the walls are breached in places, and the city is close to falling. Then a relief army arrives, and gathers on the wooded Kahlenberg hills above the city.

battle:vienna-1683:2.text: On the 12th of September, the relief army attacks. Follow the blue arrow from Poland. In the late afternoon, Sobieski leads some 18,000 horsemen, with his Winged Hussars at the front, down the hills, in one of the largest cavalry charges in history. The Ottoman army breaks, and flees. It is the high tide of Ottoman power in Europe. Sixteen years later, the Ottomans give up Hungary.

battle:blenheim.text: August 1704, on the Danube, in Bavaria. The Duke of Marlborough has marched his army 400 kilometres from the Low Countries, in secret, to save Vienna. With Prince Eugene of Savoy, he crushes the French and Bavarian army, and captures its commander. Louis the Fourteenth's run of victories is over, and Britain's rise as a great power begins. Winston Churchill's birthplace, Blenheim Palace, is named after it.

battle:poltava:0.text: This is the Battle of Poltava, fought on the 8th of July 1709, in today's Ukraine. Sweden is the great power of northern Europe, and its young king, Charles the Twelfth, is a brilliant soldier. In red is Sweden. In blue is Russia, under Peter the Great, who wants a port on the Baltic, and is building a modern army to win it.

battle:poltava:1.text: Follow the red arrows: Charles invades Russia, then turns south into Ukraine, hoping for help from the Cossacks. But the Russians burn the land ahead of him, and the winter of 1708 is one of the coldest in centuries. Thousands of Swedish soldiers freeze. In the summer of 1709, Charles besieges the town of Poltava, and Peter comes to relieve it.

battle:poltava:2.text: On the 8th of July, the Swedes attack Peter's fortified camp, against a much larger army with far more guns. Charles, wounded in the foot, directs the battle from a stretcher. By midday, his army is destroyed, and most of the survivors surrender days later. Charles escapes to Ottoman lands. Sweden's age as a great power is over, and Russia becomes the leading power of northern Europe.

battle:karnal.text: February 1739, near Delhi. Nader Shah of Persia crushes a far larger Mughal army in just three hours. In Delhi, his troops massacre tens of thousands, and he carries home the Koh-i-Noor diamond and the Peacock Throne. The Mughals' weakness is now plain for all to see, including the European trading companies.

battle:seven-years:0.text: This is the Seven Years' War, fought from 1756 to 1763 in Europe, North America, India, and on the oceans between them. Some call it the first world war. In blue are Britain and Prussia. In red are France, Austria, Russia, and later Spain. In Europe, the question is whether Prussia survives, but overseas, Britain and France are fighting to decide who will rule an empire.

battle:seven-years:1.text: The fighting has already begun in North America, where British and French colonists clash over the Ohio Valley. In 1756, Frederick the Great of Prussia invades Saxony, and in Europe a general war begins. Prussia is surrounded by enemies with far larger armies, and only British money keeps it in the fight.

battle:seven-years:2.text: Britain uses its navy to carry the war overseas. Follow the blue arrows from Britain, across the oceans. In 1759, British troops climb the cliffs at Quebec, and take the city from the French. In India, Robert Clive and the East India Company push the French aside. In Europe, Frederick wins great victories and suffers terrible defeats, and by 1762, Prussia is close to collapse. Then the Russian empress dies, and her successor, an admirer of Frederick, makes peace.

battle:seven-years:3.text: The Treaty of Paris, in 1763, gives Britain Canada and the lands east of the Mississippi, and leaves it the leading power in India. France's empire in North America is gone. Prussia keeps Silesia, and becomes a great power. About a million people have died. But the war leaves Britain deep in debt, and the new taxes it raises in America will help spark the American Revolution.

battle:plassey:0.text: Bengal, in the summer of 1757. This is India's richest province, ruled by a young nawab, Siraj ud-Daulah. In blue is the East India Company, a British trading company with its own army, led by Robert Clive. In red is the nawab's army, with French allies, some 50,000 men against the Company's 3,000. The quarrel began a year earlier, when the nawab seized the Company's fort at Calcutta. Clive has taken it back, and now he marches north. Follow the blue arrow up the river from Calcutta.

2.name: Robert Clive
2.role: Commander of the East India Company's army

battle:plassey:1.text: On the 23rd of June, the two armies meet near the village of Palashi, beside a grove of mango trees. But Clive has made a secret deal. He has promised Bengal's throne to the nawab's own commander, Mir Jafar, and when the moment comes, Mir Jafar's troops simply stand and watch. Around midday, a monsoon downpour soaks the nawab's gunpowder, while the Company keeps its own dry under cover. The nawab's guns fall silent, his army loses heart, and by evening it has fled.

battle:plassey:2.text: Siraj ud-Daulah escapes, but within days he is captured and killed. Mir Jafar becomes nawab, in name. The real power now belongs to the Company, which lost only about 22 men that day. Over the next century, it uses Bengal's wealth to spread its rule across India, and in 1858 the British Crown takes over. A short battle beside a mango grove has begun almost two centuries of British power in India.

battle:quebec-1759:0.text: This is the Battle of the Plains of Abraham, at Quebec, on the 13th of September 1759, in the Seven Years' War. Quebec is the capital of New France, the French empire in North America, perched on cliffs above the St Lawrence River. Follow the blue arrow: a British force under General James Wolfe has sailed up the river. In red is the French army of the Marquis de Montcalm.

battle:quebec-1759:1.text: All summer, Wolfe besieges the city, but cannot get past its cliffs. Then he finds a narrow path up the cliffs, upstream of the city. Before dawn on the 13th of September, his men climb it in the dark, and by morning, some 4,500 British soldiers are lined up on the plains outside the walls. Montcalm attacks at once. British volleys break the French line in less than an hour.

battle:quebec-1759:2.text: Both commanders are mortally wounded. Wolfe dies on the field, knowing he has won, and Montcalm the next morning. Quebec surrenders days later, and by 1763, France has given up Canada. But the French-speaking people of Quebec remain, and their language and culture are still a living legacy of the old colony.

battle:panipat-3:0.text: This is the Third Battle of Panipat, fought on the 14th of January 1761, north of Delhi. The Marathas, now the leading power in India, have pushed their rule as far as the Punjab. In blue are the forces of Ahmad Shah Durrani, the ruler of Afghanistan, who has come down through the passes to stop them, joined by Indian allies. In red is the great Maratha army, under Sadashivrao Bhau.

battle:panipat-3:1.text: For two months, the armies face each other at Panipat. The Afghans cut the Marathas off from their supplies, and in the Maratha camp, soldiers, horses and camp followers begin to starve. At dawn on the 14th of January, the Marathas attack. Their artillery does great damage at first, but by afternoon, Durrani sends in fresh troops, and the Maratha army collapses.

battle:panipat-3:2.text: Sadashivrao Bhau, and the young heir of the Peshwa, Vishwasrao, are killed. Up to 100,000 soldiers and camp followers may have died, in the battle and the killing that followed. Durrani soon goes home, but Maratha power in the north is broken for a decade, and the East India Company is quick to fill the gap.

battle:buxar:0.text: This is the Battle of Buxar, fought on the 22nd of October 1764, in Bihar, in eastern India. Since Plassey, the East India Company has been the real power in Bengal. In red is an alliance against it: the Mughal emperor, Shah Alam the Second, the nawab of Awadh, Shuja-ud-Daula, and Mir Qasim, the nawab of Bengal whom the Company has driven out. In blue is the Company's army, under Major Hector Munro.

battle:buxar:1.text: Follow the blue arrow west from Patna. The two armies meet near Buxar, on the banks of the Ganges. The allied army is several times larger, but its three leaders do not trust one another. The Company's disciplined infantry and artillery hold firm, and after a few hours of hard fighting, the allied army breaks, and retreats.

battle:buxar:2.text: Mir Qasim flees, and the emperor comes over to the Company's side. In 1765, by the Treaty of Allahabad, Shah Alam grants the Company the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. A trading company has become a government in all but name, and Bengal's wealth will now pay for further conquest.

battle:saratoga:0.text: These are the battles of Saratoga, fought in September and October 1777, in the forests of upstate New York. The American colonies have declared independence from Britain, but their war is going badly. In red is Britain. Its plan is to cut New England off from the other colonies, by sending an army south from Canada, down the Hudson Valley. In blue are the American rebels.

battle:saratoga:1.text: Follow the red arrow south from Quebec. General John Burgoyne's army, of British and German soldiers, sets out in the summer, but its march through the wilderness is slow, and its supplies run low. Near Saratoga, the Americans, under Horatio Gates, block its way. In two battles, in September and October, Burgoyne's attacks fail, with Benedict Arnold leading the American charge.

battle:saratoga:2.text: Surrounded and outnumbered, Burgoyne surrenders his whole army, nearly 6,000 men, on the 17th of October. The news reaches Paris, and convinces France that the Americans can win. In 1778, France allies with the United States, and a colonial revolt becomes a world war.

battle:yorktown:0.text: This is the Siege of Yorktown, in the autumn of 1781, in Virginia. The American War of Independence has gone on for six years. In red is Britain. Its general, Charles Cornwallis, has marched his army to Yorktown, on the coast, to be supplied and protected by the Royal Navy. In blue are the Americans, under George Washington, and their French allies, under the Comte de Rochambeau.

battle:yorktown:1.text: Washington sees his chance. Follow the blue arrow south from New York: the American and French armies march hundreds of kilometres to Virginia. Meanwhile, a French fleet sails up from the Caribbean, and in September, at the Battle of the Chesapeake, it drives off the British ships sent to rescue Cornwallis. Cornwallis is trapped.

battle:yorktown:2.text: The allies dig siege lines, closer and closer, and their guns pound the British defences. On the night of the 14th of October, American and French troops storm two key redoubts. On the 19th, Cornwallis surrenders his whole army. In London, the will to fight is gone. In 1783, the Treaty of Paris recognises the independence of the United States.

battle:haitian-revolution:0.text: This is the Haitian Revolution, from 1791 to 1804, on the island of Hispaniola, in the Caribbean. The western part of the island is the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the richest colony in the world, growing sugar and coffee with the forced labour of half a million enslaved Africans. In blue are the enslaved people who rise up, and their leaders, Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines. In red is France.

battle:haitian-revolution:1.text: In August 1791, on the northern plain near Cap-Français, the enslaved rise in a great revolt. Plantations burn across the north. France is in the middle of its own revolution, and in 1794 it abolishes slavery. Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved man of great skill, joins the French side, and drives out invading Spanish and British armies.

battle:haitian-revolution:2.text: By 1801, Toussaint governs the whole island. But Napoleon, now ruling France, means to restore the old colony, and in 1802 he sends a great army under his brother-in-law, General Leclerc. Follow the red arrow across the Atlantic from France. Toussaint is tricked into talks, arrested, and shipped to France, where he dies in a prison in the mountains. When it becomes clear that slavery will return, the war begins again.

battle:haitian-revolution:3.text: Yellow fever sweeps through the French army, and Leclerc himself dies. Dessalines leads the fight, and in November 1803, at Vertières, near Cap-Français, the French are defeated. On the 1st of January 1804, Dessalines declares independence, and the colony takes back an old Taíno name, Haiti. It becomes the first Black republic, and the second independent nation in the Americas. Losing the colony had already helped persuade Napoleon to sell Louisiana to the United States.

battle:valmy.text: September 1792, in Champagne. An untried army of French citizens, the new soldiers of the Revolution, faces the professional armies of Prussia and Austria. Under heavy artillery fire, they hold their ground, and the invaders turn back. The next day, France declares itself a republic. The poet Goethe, who was there, is said to have called it the beginning of a new age.

battle:nile-1798.text: August 1798, Aboukir Bay, on the coast of Egypt. Napoleon's fleet lies at anchor, thinking itself safe. At dusk, Horatio Nelson attacks from an unexpected side, between the French ships and the shore. Through the night the fleet is destroyed, and the French flagship, L'Orient, blows up. Napoleon's army is left stranded in Egypt, and Britain rules the Mediterranean.

battle:seringapatam:0.text: This is the Siege of Seringapatam, in April and May 1799, in the kingdom of Mysore, in southern India. For decades, Mysore's rulers, Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan, have fought the East India Company. Tipu has an army with a famous rocket corps, and he seeks help from the French. In red is Mysore. In blue are the Company and its ally, the Nizam of Hyderabad.

battle:seringapatam:1.text: Follow the blue arrow inland from Madras. A large Company army marches on Tipu's capital, Seringapatam, a fortress on an island in the Kaveri River. In April, the siege begins, and the Company's guns batter a breach in the walls. At midday on the 4th of May, in the heat, when the defenders least expect it, the Company's troops storm through the breach.

battle:seringapatam:2.text: Tipu Sultan dies fighting, and is found among his men near a gateway. The city is taken and plundered. The Company restores a young prince of the old Wodeyar dynasty to the throne of a smaller Mysore, under its protection. Britain's toughest rival in the south of India is gone, and Mysore's iron rockets go on to inspire the British Congreve rocket.

battle:assaye:0.text: This is the Battle of Assaye, fought on the 23rd of September 1803, in the Deccan, in western India. The Marathas are the last great Indian power that can rival the East India Company. In red are the armies of two Maratha chiefs, Daulat Rao Scindia and the Raja of Berar, with many guns, and infantry trained by European officers. In blue is the Company's army, under a young general, Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington.

battle:assaye:1.text: Follow the blue arrow north. Wellesley finds the Maratha army, far larger than his own, camped between two rivers. Rather than wait, he leads his men across the river by a ford no one has marked, and attacks its flank. The Maratha guns do terrible damage, and the Company's soldiers fall in great numbers. But they press on, and by evening, the Maratha army is driven from the field.

battle:assaye:2.text: Wellesley has lost about a third of his men. Years later, even after Waterloo, he will call Assaye his finest work in the field. More defeats follow for the Marathas that year, and British power spreads across central India. Within fifteen years, the Maratha Confederacy is broken.

battle:trafalgar:0.text: This is the Battle of Trafalgar, fought on the 21st of October 1805, off Cape Trafalgar, in the south-west of Spain. In red is the combined fleet of France and Spain, 33 ships of the line under Admiral Villeneuve. In blue is the British fleet, 27 ships under Admiral Horatio Nelson. Napoleon has gathered an army on the Channel coast to invade Britain, but first he must control the sea.

battle:trafalgar:1.text: Nelson does not form the usual line. Instead, he drives two columns of ships straight at the enemy line, to break it into pieces. Before the battle, he signals to his fleet: England expects that every man will do his duty. Watch the blue arrow. The fighting is ship against ship, at close range, for hours. At the height of it, Nelson is shot by a French marksman, on the deck of his flagship, Victory.

5.name: Horatio Nelson
5.role: Shot on the deck of Victory

battle:trafalgar:2.text: Twenty-two enemy ships are taken or destroyed, without a single British ship lost. Nelson dies below decks, knowing he has won. Napoleon's hopes of invading Britain are over. He turns instead to conquer Europe on land, but for the next hundred years, Britain's navy rules the seas.

battle:austerlitz:0.text: This is the Battle of Austerlitz, fought on the 2nd of December 1805, in Moravia, in today's Czech Republic. It is called the Battle of the Three Emperors. In blue is Napoleon, Emperor of the French. In red are the armies of the Russian Tsar, Alexander, and the Austrian Emperor, Francis, who together outnumber him.

battle:austerlitz:1.text: Napoleon sets a trap. He makes his army look weak, and leaves his right wing thin, inviting the allies to attack it. On the morning of the 2nd of December, they take the bait, and move troops down from their centre, on the Pratzen Heights, to strike his right. Then, as the sun burns through the fog, Napoleon's men storm up the heights, and split the allied army in two.

battle:austerlitz:2.text: By evening, the allied army is shattered, and some flee across frozen ponds. Austria makes peace, and Russia withdraws. Within a year, the Holy Roman Empire, a thousand years old, is dissolved. Austerlitz is still taught as a masterpiece of battlefield deception.

battle:borodino:0.text: This is the Battle of Borodino, fought on the 7th of September 1812, west of Moscow. Napoleon has invaded Russia with the largest army Europe has ever seen, more than 500,000 men. In blue is his Grande Armée. In red is the Russian army, which has retreated for weeks, burning the land behind it. Now its commander, Mikhail Kutuzov, makes a stand.

battle:borodino:1.text: Follow the blue arrow east from Vilnius. Near the village of Borodino, the two armies meet, a quarter of a million men in all. From dawn, Napoleon's troops attack the Russian earthworks, above all the Great Redoubt, which changes hands again and again. The cannon fire never stops. By evening, the Russians fall back, but in good order.

battle:borodino:2.text: It is one of the bloodiest single days of fighting in history. Some 30,000 French and 45,000 Russians are killed or wounded. A week later, Napoleon enters Moscow, only to find it empty, and soon burning. Russia will not make peace. In October, he retreats through the Russian winter, and of the great army that invaded, only a small fraction marches home.

battle:leipzig:0.text: This is the Battle of Leipzig, fought from the 16th to the 19th of October 1813, in Saxony. It is called the Battle of the Nations. After the disaster in Russia, Napoleon has raised a new army. In red is France, with its remaining German allies. In blue are Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden, united against him at last.

battle:leipzig:1.text: Watch the blue arrows: the allied armies converge on Leipzig from the north, east and south. Almost 600,000 soldiers fight for four days, in the largest battle in Europe before the First World War. Napoleon's forces are slowly pressed back toward the city. Some of his Saxon troops change sides in the middle of the battle.

battle:leipzig:2.text: On the 19th, Napoleon orders a retreat over the River Elster. But the only bridge is blown up too early, trapping thousands of his men on the wrong side. Tens of thousands of French soldiers are killed, wounded or captured. Napoleon is driven out of Germany, and within six months, the allies are in Paris, and he gives up his throne.

battle:waterloo:0.text: This is the Battle of Waterloo, fought on the 18th of June 1815, near Brussels. Napoleon has escaped from exile on the island of Elba, and taken back the throne of France. In red is his French army. In blue are the armies of Britain and the Netherlands, under the Duke of Wellington, and of Prussia, under Marshal Blücher. Napoleon's plan is to beat them one at a time, before they can join.

battle:waterloo:1.text: Watch the red arrow from the south. Wellington's army waits along a low ridge, partly hidden behind its crest. All day, Napoleon throws attack after attack at it: infantry, cannon, and great charges of cavalry against squares of British infantry. The farm of Hougoumont holds out, though it burns. In the evening, the Prussians arrive on Napoleon's flank. Then even the Imperial Guard falls back.

battle:waterloo:2.text: The French army breaks and flees. Some 33,000 French, and 24,000 of their enemies, have been killed or wounded. Napoleon gives up his throne for the second time, and is sent to the remote island of Saint Helena, in the South Atlantic, where he dies in 1821. Twenty-three years of war in Europe are over, and a century begins in which Britain is the world's leading power.

battle:boyaca.text: August 1819, in Colombia. Simón Bolívar leads his army over a freezing Andean pass, in the rainy season, a crossing the Spanish thought impossible. He surprises them at a bridge at Boyacá, and three days later, Bogotá falls. It is the beginning of the end of Spain's empire in the Americas.

battle:ayacucho.text: December 1824, high in the Andes of Peru. Antonio José de Sucre's patriot army destroys the last royal army in South America, and captures the viceroy himself. Three centuries of Spanish rule on the South American mainland are over. Soon after, a new country is founded, and named after Bolívar: Bolivia.

battle:navarino.text: October 1827, Navarino Bay, in south-west Greece. The fleets of Britain, France and Russia enter the bay to enforce a truce in the Greek war of independence. A shot is fired, a battle begins, and within four hours, the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet is gone. Greek independence is secured.

battle:opium-war:0.text: This is the First Opium War, fought from 1839 to 1842 between Britain and the Qing Empire of China. In blue is Britain, the world's greatest naval power. In red is Qing China. British merchants buy tea, silk and porcelain from China, and to pay for them, they smuggle in opium grown in British India. Great numbers of Chinese become addicted, and silver drains out of the country.

battle:opium-war:1.text: In 1839, the emperor sends a determined official, Lin Zexu, to Canton, to stop the trade. He blockades the foreign merchants, seizes their opium, more than 1,000 tonnes of it, and has it destroyed. Britain answers with warships. Follow the blue arrow from Singapore to the coast near Hong Kong.

battle:opium-war:2.text: Steam-powered gunboats, such as the iron-hulled Nemesis, sail up China's rivers, and the old Qing forts and war junks cannot stop them. The British take the forts of Canton, then Chusan, Amoy and Ningbo. In 1842 they sail up the Yangtze and take Zhenjiang, cutting the Grand Canal, China's great artery for grain. Follow the blue arrows up the coast to the great river.

battle:opium-war:3.text: With Nanking under threat, China signs the Treaty of Nanking, in August 1842. It hands Hong Kong island to Britain, opens five ports to foreign trade, and pays a large sum in silver. It is the first of the treaties that China would call unequal. China remembers it as the beginning of a century of humiliation, and it marks the start of the long decline of the Qing.

battle:mexican-american:0.text: This is the Mexican-American War, fought from 1846 to 1848. In blue is the United States, young, fast-growing, and eager to reach the Pacific. In red is Mexico, independent for only 25 years, and divided by politics. Between them lies a vast land, from Texas to California, much of it thinly settled. Watch the map: by the end of this war, that land will change hands.

battle:mexican-american:1.text: Texas had broken away from Mexico in 1836, and in 1845 the United States annexes it. The two countries also disagree about the border: the Nueces River, or the Rio Grande. President James Polk sends troops under Zachary Taylor to the Rio Grande, and in 1846, after a clash there, the United States declares war.

battle:mexican-american:2.text: Taylor pushes south into northern Mexico, and wins at Monterrey and Buena Vista. Follow the blue arrow inland from the Rio Grande. Meanwhile, American forces take New Mexico and California. Then, in March 1847, Winfield Scott lands an army at Veracruz, and fights his way up to Mexico City, along the old road of the conquistadors. In September, the capital falls.

battle:mexican-american:3.text: In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, in 1848, Mexico gives up a vast territory: California, and much of today's American south-west. The United States now stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Just days before the treaty is signed, gold had been found in California. But the quarrel over whether slavery may spread into the new lands will push the country toward civil war.

battle:taiping:0.text: This is the Taiping Rebellion, fought in China from 1850 to 1864, one of the deadliest wars in history. In blue is the Qing Empire, which has ruled China for two centuries. The red arrow marks its enemy, the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. Its leader is Hong Xiuquan, a failed candidate in the imperial exams, who came to believe, after a series of visions, that he was the younger brother of Jesus.

battle:taiping:1.text: The rising breaks out at the start of 1851, in the hills of Guangxi, in the far south, among poor farmers, miners and charcoal-burners. Hong's followers ban opium, gambling and foot-binding, and promise land and equality. Follow the red arrow north. Their army grows to hundreds of thousands, and in 1853 they capture the great city of Nanjing, and make it their Heavenly Capital.

battle:taiping:2.text: For a decade, the Taiping rule much of southern and central China from Nanjing. The fighting sweeps across whole provinces, and towns change hands again and again. The Qing's old armies fail, so scholar-officials such as Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang raise new provincial armies. Western-led forces, among them the Ever Victorious Army, help defend Shanghai. Meanwhile, the Taiping leaders quarrel, and in 1856 they turn on one another.

battle:taiping:3.text: In 1864, Zeng Guofan's Hunan Army closes in on Nanjing. Hong Xiuquan dies during the siege, and in July the city falls. Between 20 and 30 million people have died, more than in the First World War, many of them from famine and disease. Whole provinces are left empty. The Qing survive, but power has shifted to regional generals, and the dynasty never recovers its strength.

battle:crimean:0.text: This is the Crimean War, fought from 1853 to 1856. In red is the Russian Empire, pushing south against the weakening Ottoman Empire. In blue are the Ottomans and their allies, Britain and France, later joined by the Kingdom of Sardinia. Britain and France fear that if the Ottomans collapse, Russia will control the way into the Mediterranean. Watch the map: the war's great prize is the Crimean peninsula, in the Black Sea.

battle:crimean:1.text: The quarrel starts with a dispute over the rights of Christians in the Holy Land. In 1853, Russia occupies the Danube provinces, and its fleet destroys an Ottoman squadron at Sinop. In 1854, Britain and France declare war. Their armies sail across the Black Sea, and land in Crimea, to take the great Russian naval base at Sevastopol. Follow the blue arrow across the sea.

battle:crimean:2.text: The siege of Sevastopol lasts almost a year. At Balaclava, a misunderstood order sends British light cavalry charging into a valley ringed with Russian guns: the Charge of the Light Brigade. Through the winter, the soldiers freeze in their trenches, and disease kills far more of them than battle. News reaches home faster than ever before, and in a hospital at Scutari, Florence Nightingale begins to change nursing for good.

battle:crimean:3.text: In September 1855, French troops storm the Malakhov fortress, and the Russians leave Sevastopol. The Treaty of Paris, in 1856, forbids warships on the Black Sea, and keeps the Ottoman Empire standing. Between half a million and 750,000 people have died. Russia's defeat exposes how far it has fallen behind, and within a few years, it frees its serfs.

battle:indian-rebellion:0.text: This is the Indian Rebellion of 1857, which many in India remember as the First War of Independence. By now, the East India Company, a British trading company with its own armies, rules much of India. In blue are the Company and British forces. In red are the rebels: Indian soldiers of the Company's own army, and the princes, landlords and peasants who join them. Watch the map around Delhi, where it all comes to a head.

battle:indian-rebellion:1.text: In 1857, a new rifle reaches the Company's Indian soldiers, the sepoys. Its cartridges are said to be greased with cow and pig fat, an offence to Hindus and Muslims alike. In May, at Meerut, soldiers who refuse them are jailed, and their comrades rise up. Follow the red arrow: they ride to Delhi, and proclaim the aged Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, as their leader.

battle:indian-rebellion:2.text: The rising spreads across northern and central India. At Kanpur and Lucknow, British garrisons are besieged, and there are terrible massacres, by both sides. In September, after a long siege, British and loyal Indian troops storm Delhi. Follow the blue arrow from the Punjab. In central India, the Rani of Jhansi rides into battle at the head of her troops, and dies fighting in 1858.

battle:indian-rebellion:3.text: By 1858, the rebellion is crushed. The last Mughal emperor is exiled to Burma, and the dynasty ends. The British government abolishes the East India Company's rule, and the Crown takes direct control of India: the British Raj begins. In India, the rising came to be remembered as an early fight for freedom, the first stirring of a long struggle for independence.

battle:solferino.text: June 1859, in Lombardy. Three monarchs lead their armies in person, and some 270,000 men fight through a long, hot day. A Swiss businessman passing by, Henry Dunant, is so shocked by the thousands of wounded left to die that he goes on to found the Red Cross. The battle is a great step towards a united Italy, and leads to the first Geneva Convention.

battle:american-civil-war:0.text: This is the American Civil War, fought from 1861 to 1865. In blue is the Union, the government of President Abraham Lincoln, with the states of the north. Against it stands the Confederacy: eleven southern states that break away to protect slavery, led by Jefferson Davis, with Robert E. Lee as their greatest general. Watch the map: much of the fighting is in Virginia, between the two capitals, Washington and Richmond, barely 160 kilometres apart.

battle:american-civil-war:1.text: Abraham Lincoln is elected president in November 1860, opposed to slavery spreading into new lands. Within months, seven southern states declare that they are leaving the Union, and four more follow. In April 1861, Confederate guns open fire on Fort Sumter, in Charleston harbour. Both sides expect a short war.

battle:american-civil-war:2.text: It is not short. Huge armies, moved by railway and armed with rifles, fight battles that cost tens of thousands of lives. In 1863, Lincoln declares the enslaved people of the Confederacy free, and that July, the Union wins at Gettysburg, and takes Vicksburg on the Mississippi. Then Ulysses Grant presses Lee in Virginia, while William Sherman marches through Georgia to the sea. Follow the blue arrows.

battle:american-civil-war:3.text: In April 1865, Richmond falls, and at Appomattox Court House, Lee surrenders to Grant. Days later, Lincoln is assassinated. Between 620,000 and 750,000 people have died. Slavery is ended throughout the United States, and the country comes out of the war as one nation, under a stronger federal government.

battle:gettysburg:0.text: This is the Battle of Gettysburg, fought from the 1st to the 3rd of July 1863, in the American Civil War. In blue is the Union's Army of the Potomac, under General George Meade. Against it is the Confederate army of Robert E. Lee. After victories in Virginia, Lee has marched north into Pennsylvania, hoping a win on Northern soil will break the North's will to fight. Follow the arrows: both armies converge on a small country town.

battle:gettysburg:1.text: On the first day, the Confederates drive the Union troops back through the town, to the hills south of it. On the second, Lee attacks both ends of the Union line, at Little Round Top and Culp's Hill, and is held off. On the third day, after a huge artillery barrage, some 12,500 Confederates march across open fields toward the centre of the line, in what is known as Pickett's Charge. It is cut to pieces.

battle:gettysburg:2.text: Lee retreats to Virginia. More than 45,000 men have been killed, wounded, captured or gone missing, the most of any battle of the war. The South never again invades the North in force, and the next day, Vicksburg falls in the west. That November, Lincoln comes here to dedicate a cemetery, and gives the Gettysburg Address.

battle:paraguayan-war:0.text: This is the Paraguayan War, sometimes called the War of the Triple Alliance, fought from 1864 to 1870. In red is Paraguay, a small inland country ruled by Francisco Solano López, with one of the largest armies in South America. In blue are its three neighbours, Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, allied against it. Watch the map: the war is fought along the great rivers, the Paraná and the Paraguay, Paraguay's only road to the sea.

battle:paraguayan-war:1.text: The trouble begins in Uruguay, where Brazil intervenes in a civil war in 1864. López sees a threat to Paraguay's survival, and strikes first. He seizes a Brazilian ship, invades the Brazilian province of Mato Grosso, and then sends his army across Argentine territory. In 1865, Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay sign the Treaty of the Triple Alliance.

battle:paraguayan-war:2.text: The allies push the Paraguayans back, and the war moves onto Paraguay's own soil. Follow the blue arrows up the rivers. For years, the allies are held at the riverside fortress of Humaitá, until it falls in 1868. Paraguayans fight on with extraordinary stubbornness, and as the men are killed, boys and old men take their place. Disease and hunger take as many lives as the fighting.

battle:paraguayan-war:3.text: In 1869, the allies take the capital, Asunción. López retreats into the north-east with the last of his army, and in March 1870 he is killed at Cerro Corá. Paraguay is devastated. It may have lost half its people, and most of its men. Brazil's army comes home powerful, and its officers will help end the Brazilian monarchy in 1889.

battle:koniggratz.text: July 1866, in Bohemia. The Prussian general Helmuth von Moltke brings three armies by railway to meet on the battlefield. Prussian breech-loading rifles fire several times faster than the Austrian muzzle-loaders. Austria loses the war in just seven weeks, and is pushed out of German affairs. The way is now clear for a German Empire, led by Prussia.

battle:sedan:0.text: This is the Battle of Sedan, fought on the 1st and 2nd of September 1870, in north-eastern France. France, under Emperor Napoleon the Third, has declared war on Prussia, which leads the German states. In blue are Prussia and its German allies, with a fast-moving, well-organised army, under Helmuth von Moltke. In red is France.

battle:sedan:1.text: The Germans win a string of battles, and trap one French army in the fortress of Metz. A second French army, with the emperor himself, marches to rescue it, but is caught near the town of Sedan, by the Belgian border. Follow the blue arrow. German armies close in from all sides, and their artillery, on the hills around, pounds the French in the valley below.

battle:sedan:2.text: On the 2nd of September, Napoleon the Third surrenders, with more than 100,000 men. In Paris, a republic is declared, and the war goes on, but in January 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the German Empire is proclaimed. France loses Alsace and part of Lorraine, and the bitterness between the two nations will feed the World Wars.

battle:little-bighorn:0.text: This is the Battle of the Little Bighorn, fought in June 1876, in what is now Montana. Gold has been found in the Black Hills, sacred to the Lakota, and land promised to them by treaty. The United States Army is sent to force the Lakota and their allies onto reservations. The red arrow is the army. Against it are the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho, gathered around leaders such as Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse.

battle:little-bighorn:1.text: On the 25th of June, Lieutenant Colonel George Custer and the 7th Cavalry find a huge camp along the Little Bighorn River, perhaps thousands of people. Follow the red arrow. Custer does not wait. He splits his regiment, and attacks. The warriors drive back one attack, and then turn on Custer's own column, on the hills above the river.

battle:little-bighorn:2.text: Custer, and all of the more than 200 men with him, are killed. It is the greatest Native American victory of the Plains Wars. But the army returns in force, and within a year, most of the Lakota and their allies are forced onto reservations. Sitting Bull leads his people into Canada, and Crazy Horse surrenders, and is killed in custody.

battle:isandlwana:0.text: This is the Battle of Isandlwana, fought on the 22nd of January 1879, in southern Africa. In red is Britain, which wants to bring the region under its control. In blue is the Zulu Kingdom, under King Cetshwayo, with a disciplined army of tens of thousands of warriors. Britain sends an ultimatum, demanding that the Zulu army be disbanded. Cetshwayo cannot accept it, and British troops cross into Zululand.

battle:isandlwana:1.text: The British commander, Lord Chelmsford, leaves part of his force in a camp beneath the hill of Isandlwana, and rides off to find the Zulu army. But the main Zulu army, some 20,000 strong, is hidden in a valley nearby. Follow the blue arrow. Around midday, it attacks, spreading out in the famous horns of the buffalo, to surround the camp.

battle:isandlwana:2.text: The camp is overrun. More than 1,300 of its defenders are killed, one of the worst defeats a modern army has suffered at the hands of an indigenous force. That night, a small British garrison holds the mission at Rorke's Drift. Britain sends more troops, and in July, at Ulundi, the Zulu army is defeated, and the royal kraal is burned. Within months, the Zulu kingdom is broken up.

battle:war-of-the-pacific:0.text: This is the War of the Pacific, fought from 1879 to 1884. In blue is Chile. In red are Peru and Bolivia, allies by a secret treaty. Watch the map: the war is fought over the Atacama, the driest desert on Earth, along the Pacific coast. At this time, Bolivia has a coastline here, and the desert holds a fortune in nitrates, prized for fertiliser and explosives.

battle:war-of-the-pacific:1.text: Chilean companies mine the nitrates in Bolivia's coastal province. In 1878, Bolivia raises a tax on them, against an earlier agreement, and when the companies refuse to pay, it moves to seize their property. In February 1879, Chilean troops occupy the port of Antofagasta. Follow the blue arrow north from Valparaíso. Peru, bound by its treaty with Bolivia, is drawn in.

battle:war-of-the-pacific:2.text: First, the war is fought at sea. The Peruvian ironclad Huáscar, under Admiral Miguel Grau, raids the Chilean coast for months, until in October 1879 it is cornered and captured at the Battle of Angamos. Grau dies on his bridge. With the sea in its hands, Chile lands armies in the desert, and takes the nitrate provinces one by one.

battle:war-of-the-pacific:3.text: In January 1881, Chilean troops enter Lima, Peru's capital. Peruvian resistance, led by Andrés Cáceres, fights on in the mountains for two more years. Peace comes with Peru in 1883, and in 1884 Bolivia agrees a truce. Chile gains the nitrate lands and grows rich, and Bolivia loses its whole coastline. Bolivia has been landlocked ever since, yet it still keeps a navy, on Lake Titicaca.

battle:adwa:0.text: This is the Battle of Adwa, fought on the 1st of March 1896, in the mountains of northern Ethiopia. European powers are carving up Africa. In red is Italy, which holds the colony of Eritrea, on the Red Sea, and means to make Ethiopia its protectorate. In blue is Ethiopia, under Emperor Menelik the Second, and his wife, Empress Taytu.

battle:adwa:1.text: The quarrel is over a treaty. In the Italian version, Ethiopia has agreed to become a protectorate. In the Amharic version, it has not. Menelik rejects the Italian claim, and gathers a huge army from across his empire, well armed with modern rifles and artillery. Follow the blue arrow north from Addis Ababa.

battle:adwa:2.text: Before dawn on the 1st of March, the Italian columns advance through the mountains toward Adwa. In the darkness and broken ground, they lose touch with one another, and Menelik's army falls on them one by one. By midday, the Italian army is destroyed. Italy recognises Ethiopia's independence, and Ethiopia stays free through the scramble for Africa, a symbol of African freedom ever since.

battle:omdurman.text: September 1898, on the Nile, in Sudan. Herbert Kitchener's army has Maxim machine guns and river gunboats. In a single morning, wave after wave of Sudanese soldiers are cut down: about 10,000 killed, against fewer than 50 on the British side. A young Winston Churchill rides in one of the last British cavalry charges. It is a grim picture of the industrial firepower behind colonial conquest.

battle:spanish-american:0.text: This is the Spanish-American War, fought in 1898. In blue is the United States, a rising power. In red is Spain, whose empire once spanned the world, and which still holds Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines. Cuban rebels have been fighting for independence for years, and Americans follow their struggle in the newspapers.

battle:spanish-american:1.text: In February 1898, the American battleship Maine explodes and sinks in Havana harbour, killing more than 260 sailors. The cause is never settled, but American newspapers blame Spain. In April, the United States declares war.

battle:spanish-american:2.text: The first blow falls on the other side of the world. Follow the blue arrow from Hong Kong. On the 1st of May, Commodore George Dewey's squadron sails into Manila Bay, and destroys the Spanish fleet in a single morning. In Cuba, American troops land near Santiago, and Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders charge up San Juan Hill. In July, the Spanish fleet tries to break out of Santiago harbour, and is destroyed.

battle:spanish-american:3.text: By August, the fighting is over, after barely four months. In the Treaty of Paris, Spain gives up Cuba, and hands Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States. Four centuries of Spain's empire across the oceans come to an end. The United States emerges as a world power, with an empire of its own, and in the Philippines a new war soon begins, against Filipinos fighting for independence.

battle:boer-war:0.text: This is the Second Boer War, fought in South Africa from 1899 to 1902. In blue is the British Empire, which rules the Cape Colony and Natal. In red are two small republics of the Boers, farmers descended from Dutch settlers: the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. Beneath the Transvaal lies the richest gold field in the world, discovered in 1886, near what is now Johannesburg.

battle:boer-war:1.text: Thousands of foreign miners, many of them British, pour into the Transvaal, and Britain demands rights for them. The Transvaal's president, Paul Kruger, sees a threat to Boer independence. In October 1899, the Boers strike first. They invade Natal and the Cape, and besiege the towns of Ladysmith, Kimberley and Mafeking.

battle:boer-war:2.text: In December, in what the British call Black Week, three British armies are beaten in a few days. Britain sends huge reinforcements under Lord Roberts. Follow the blue arrows inland from the coast. The sieges are lifted, and in 1900 the British take Bloemfontein, Johannesburg and Pretoria. But the war is not over. Boer commandos on horseback, under leaders such as Christiaan de Wet, fight on as guerrillas.

battle:boer-war:3.text: Lord Kitchener answers by burning farms, and moving Boer families, and Black Africans, into camps. Disease and hunger in the camps kill more than 26,000 Boer women and children, and at least 14,000 Black Africans, probably more. In May 1902, the Boers agree to peace at Vereeniging. In 1910, the Union of South Africa is formed, on terms that leave most of the Black majority without a vote.

battle:tsushima:0.text: This is the Battle of Tsushima, fought in May 1905, in the strait between Korea and Japan. Russia and Japan are at war over Manchuria and Korea. In red is Russia, whose Pacific fleet has been trapped and destroyed at Port Arthur. In blue is Japan, with a modern navy under Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō.

battle:tsushima:1.text: So Russia sends its Baltic Fleet halfway around the world. Follow the red arrows. It sails from the Baltic, around Africa, and across the Indian Ocean, a voyage of seven months and some 30,000 kilometres, taking on coal as it goes. In May 1905, it tries to slip through the Tsushima Strait, to reach Vladivostok.

battle:tsushima:2.text: Tōgō is waiting. On the 27th of May, he turns his battleships across the head of the Russian line, and pours fire into each Russian ship as it comes. In two days, almost the whole Russian fleet is sunk or captured, while Japan loses only three torpedo boats. It is the first time in the modern age that an Asian power has beaten a European great power. Russia makes peace, and at home, its revolution of 1905 deepens.

battle:mexican-revolution:0.text: This is the Mexican Revolution, a decade of upheaval from 1910 to 1920. For over 30 years, Mexico has been ruled by Porfirio Díaz. The country has railways and foreign investment, but most of the land belongs to a few great estates, and the villagers who work it are poor. The revolutionaries are shown in blue. Watch the map: the fighting will run from the northern deserts to the villages south of Mexico City.

battle:mexican-revolution:1.text: In 1910, Díaz claims victory in yet another election, and a wealthy reformer, Francisco Madero, calls for revolt. In the north, Pancho Villa raises an army of cowboys and miners. In the south, in Morelos, Emiliano Zapata leads villagers fighting for their land. In 1911, Díaz resigns and leaves for exile, and Madero becomes president.

battle:mexican-revolution:2.text: But peace does not come. In 1913, General Victoriano Huerta seizes power, and Madero is murdered. Villa, Zapata and Venustiano Carranza unite against Huerta, and drive him out. Follow the blue arrow from Chihuahua to Zacatecas. Then the victors turn on one another. Carranza's armies defeat Villa, and the fighting drags on for years.

battle:mexican-revolution:3.text: In 1917, a new constitution promises land reform and the rights of workers. Zapata is lured into an ambush and killed in 1919, and Carranza himself is killed in 1920. By then, perhaps a million people have died. The revolution's leaders are gone, but its ideas shape Mexico for the rest of the century, and Zapata and Villa become legends.

battle:xinhai:0.text: This is the Xinhai Revolution, which brought down China's last imperial dynasty in 1911 and 1912. For more than two and a half centuries, China has been ruled by the Qing. Now the empire is weak, humiliated by foreign powers, and many Chinese want a modern republic. The revolutionaries are shown in blue. Their best-known leader is Sun Yat-sen, a doctor who has spent years in exile, raising money for the cause.

battle:xinhai:1.text: In October 1911, in Hankou, across the river from the city of Wuchang, a bomb goes off by accident in a revolutionaries' hideout. Police find lists of names, and to save themselves, soldiers in Wuchang mutiny, and take the city. Within weeks, province after province declares itself independent of the Qing.

battle:xinhai:2.text: The rebels take Nanjing, the old southern capital. Follow the blue arrow down the river. Sun Yat-sen hurries home from abroad, and on the 1st of January 1912, in Nanjing, he is sworn in as the first president of the Republic of China. In Beijing, the court turns to its strongest general, Yuan Shikai, to save it.

battle:xinhai:3.text: Yuan makes a deal with the revolutionaries instead. In February 1912, the six-year-old emperor, Puyi, gives up the throne, and more than 2,000 years of imperial rule in China come to an end. Sun Yat-sen steps aside, and Yuan becomes president. But the new republic is fragile, and China enters decades of warlords, civil war and invasion.

battle:balkan-wars:0.text: These are the Balkan Wars, fought in 1912 and 1913. For five centuries, the Ottoman Empire has ruled most of south-eastern Europe. By now, it holds only a band of land across the middle of the peninsula, from the Adriatic to Constantinople. In blue are four small kingdoms, Serbia, Greece, Bulgaria and Montenegro, which have formed the Balkan League. In red is the Ottoman Empire.

battle:balkan-wars:1.text: In October 1912, the League attacks. Watch the blue arrows close in from three sides. The Bulgarians drive the Ottomans back toward Constantinople, the Serbs sweep south into Macedonia, and the Greeks take the port of Salonika. In just a few weeks, the Ottoman armies in Europe are shattered.

battle:balkan-wars:2.text: The great powers broker a peace in London in 1913, and Albania becomes an independent state. But the victors cannot agree how to share the land they have won, above all Macedonia. In June 1913, Bulgaria attacks its former allies, Serbia and Greece. Romania and the Ottomans join in against it, and within weeks, Bulgaria is beaten.

battle:balkan-wars:3.text: By the Treaty of Bucharest, in August 1913, Serbia and Greece gain most of Macedonia, and the Ottomans keep only a corner of Europe around Constantinople. Five centuries of Ottoman rule in most of the Balkans are over. But Serbia, now larger and more confident, alarms its neighbour, Austria-Hungary. Less than a year later, a young Bosnian Serb fires the shots in Sarajevo that begin the First World War.

battle:marne:0.text: This is the First Battle of the Marne, fought east of Paris, in September 1914. A month into the First World War, Germany has put its great plan into action: to sweep through Belgium and around Paris, and defeat France in six weeks, before turning on Russia. In red, the German armies march south. In blue are France and Britain, retreating day after day.

battle:marne:1.text: By early September, German troops are within about 50 kilometres of Paris. Follow the red arrow from Belgium. But one German army has turned too soon, and a gap opens between it and its neighbour. On the 6th of September, the French commander, Joseph Joffre, counter-attacks, and the British push into the gap. Some French soldiers are even rushed to the front in Paris taxis.

battle:marne:2.text: The German commanders lose their nerve, and on the 9th of September they order a retreat, back to the River Aisne, where they dig in. The hope of a quick victory is over. Soon, a line of trenches stretches from the North Sea to Switzerland, and it will barely move for almost four years.

battle:gallipoli:0.text: This is the Gallipoli campaign, fought from April 1915 to January 1916. The Ottoman Empire has joined Germany in the First World War. In red are Britain and France, with soldiers from Australia and New Zealand, the Anzacs. They plan to force the narrow Dardanelles strait, take Constantinople, and knock the Ottomans out of the war. In blue is the Ottoman Empire.

battle:gallipoli:1.text: In March, an Allied fleet tries to force the strait, but loses ships to mines. So on the 25th of April, troops land on the Gallipoli peninsula. Follow the red arrows. The British land at its southern tip, and the Anzacs at a narrow cove beneath steep cliffs. On the heights above, a young Ottoman officer, Mustafa Kemal, rallies his men, and they hold the ridges.

battle:gallipoli:2.text: For eight months, the two sides fight from trenches only metres apart, in summer heat and swarms of flies, and then winter storms. Disease spreads through the Allied camps. A new landing at Suvla Bay, in August, fails to break the deadlock. In December and January, the Allies withdraw, by night, with almost no losses. Around half a million men have been killed, wounded or fallen sick. Mustafa Kemal goes on to found modern Turkey, and Anzac Day is still kept in Australia and New Zealand.

battle:verdun:0.text: This is the Battle of Verdun, fought in north-eastern France, through almost all of 1916. Verdun is a fortress city, ringed by forts, on the River Meuse. In red is Germany. Its commander, Erich von Falkenhayn, chooses to attack here, believing France will defend it at any cost, and wear out its army doing so. In blue is France.

battle:verdun:1.text: On the 21st of February, after a bombardment from more than 1,000 guns, the Germans attack. Follow the red arrow. Within days, they take the great Fort Douaumont. General Philippe Pétain takes command, and keeps Verdun supplied along a single road, the Sacred Way, where trucks run day and night. The French rallying cry is: They shall not pass.

battle:verdun:2.text: For ten months, the two armies fight over a few square kilometres of shattered ground. Villages are wiped off the map, and the forests turn to mud and stumps. By December, the French have retaken most of what was lost. More than 700,000 men have been killed, wounded or gone missing. Verdun becomes a lasting symbol of French resolve, and of the waste of a war of attrition.

battle:jutland.text: May 1916, in the North Sea. About 250 warships of the British and German fleets meet in the largest naval battle of the war. Britain loses more ships and more men. Yet afterwards, the German fleet barely challenges it again, turning instead to submarines. And it is the U-boats that will bring the United States into the war.

battle:somme:0.text: This is the Battle of the Somme, fought in northern France, from July to November 1916. Since 1914, the armies of the Western Front have faced each other across lines of trenches. In blue are Britain and France, whose attack here is meant to break through, and to take pressure off the French at Verdun. In red is Germany, dug into deep, strong defences on the chalk ridges above the river.

battle:somme:1.text: For a week, British guns fire more than a million and a half shells at the German lines. Then, on the 1st of July, at 7:30 in the morning, the whistles blow, and the British infantry climbs out of the trenches. But the shells have not cut the wire, and the Germans have survived in their deep dugouts. Their machine guns open fire. On that one day, the British Army suffers some 57,000 casualties, nearly 20,000 of them killed.

battle:somme:2.text: Still the battle goes on, for four and a half months. In September, tanks go into battle for the first time in history. When the winter rains turn the ground to mud, the offensive ends. The Allies have advanced about 10 kilometres. More than a million men on both sides have been killed or wounded, and the Somme becomes a byword for the horror of the Great War.

battle:russian-civil-war:0.text: This is the Russian Civil War, fought from 1917 to 1922, across the whole of the old Russian Empire. The Bolsheviks, known as the Reds, are shown here in blue: Lenin's communists, who seized power in the October Revolution. The red arrows belong to their enemies, the White armies, a mix of monarchists, officers and moderates, helped for a time by foreign troops. The war is fought across a land that stretches from the Baltic to the Pacific.

battle:russian-civil-war:1.text: In October 1917, the Bolsheviks take power in Petrograd, and soon move the capital to Moscow. Follow the blue arrow. In 1918, they make peace with Germany, giving up vast lands in the west, and armies rise against them on every side. A legion of Czechoslovak soldiers seizes the Trans-Siberian Railway, and in the summer of 1918, the former tsar and his family are shot.

battle:russian-civil-war:2.text: Leon Trotsky builds the Red Army, and races between the fronts in an armoured train. In 1919, the Whites come close. Admiral Kolchak advances from Siberia, and General Denikin pushes north from the south, toward Moscow. Watch the red arrows. But the Whites are divided and spread thin, while the Reds hold the centre, with its railways and factories. Both advances are thrown back.

battle:russian-civil-war:3.text: By 1920, the Whites are beaten, and their last army leaves Crimea by sea. Fighting goes on at the edges for two more years. Between 7 and 12 million people have died, far more from famine and disease than from battle. In December 1922, the Bolsheviks found the Soviet Union, the world's first communist state, and it will shape the whole of the 20th century.

battle:turkish-independence:0.text: This is the Turkish War of Independence, fought from 1919 to 1923. The Ottoman Empire has lost the First World War, and the Allies are carving up its lands. In blue are the Turkish nationalists, led by an Ottoman general, Mustafa Kemal, later called Atatürk. In red is Greece, whose army lands in Anatolia with the backing of the Allies.

battle:turkish-independence:1.text: In May 1919, a Greek army lands at Smyrna, today's İzmir, on the Aegean coast. Days later, Mustafa Kemal sails to the Black Sea coast, and begins to rally resistance. In 1920, the sultan's government signs the Treaty of Sèvres, which would leave the Turks only a small part of Anatolia. The nationalists reject it, and set up their own government in Ankara.

battle:turkish-independence:2.text: The Greek army advances deep into Anatolia. Follow the red arrow inland from İzmir. In the summer of 1921, it comes close to Ankara, and on the Sakarya River, the Turks stop it, after three weeks of fighting. A year later, in August 1922, Kemal launches a great offensive, and the Greek army collapses. Follow the blue arrow back to the sea.

battle:turkish-independence:3.text: In September 1922, Turkish troops enter İzmir, and much of the city burns. The Treaty of Lausanne, in 1923, replaces the Treaty of Sèvres, and recognises the borders of a new Turkey. More than a million Greeks and around 400,000 Muslims are forced to leave their homes, in an exchange of populations. The sultanate is abolished, and in October 1923, Turkey becomes a republic, with Mustafa Kemal as its first president.

battle:warsaw-1920.text: August 1920. Soviet armies are at the gates of Warsaw, and Poland's newly won independence seems about to end. Then Józef Piłsudski strikes from the south, into a gap in the Soviet line. The Red Army collapses. Poland survives, and the revolution is kept from spreading west by force of arms.

battle:spanish-civil-war:0.text: This is the Spanish Civil War, fought from 1936 to 1939. On the map, Spain is shaded blue for the Nationalists, led by General Francisco Franco, with their backers, Hitler's Germany and Mussolini's Italy. In red is the Soviet Union, which backs the other side: the elected government of the Spanish Republic. Spain is deeply divided, between left and right, town and country.

battle:spanish-civil-war:1.text: In July 1936, army officers rise against the Republic. The coup fails in Madrid and Barcelona, and Spain splits in two. Franco's best troops are in Morocco, across the sea, and German and Italian planes help fly them over to Spain. Follow the blue arrows from Africa to Seville, and on toward Madrid.

battle:spanish-civil-war:2.text: The Nationalists reach the edge of Madrid in November 1936, but the city holds. Volunteers come from around the world to fight for the Republic, in the International Brigades, while the Soviet Union sends it weapons. In April 1937, German bombers destroy the Basque town of Guernica, and Picasso's painting of it shocks the world. Slowly, the Nationalists gain ground.

battle:spanish-civil-war:3.text: In 1938, the Republic's last great offensive, on the Ebro, fails. Barcelona falls in January 1939, and Madrid at the end of March. Around half a million people have died, in battle, in bombing, and in killings behind the lines on both sides. Franco rules Spain as a dictator until his death in 1975. Within months of the war's end, Europe is at war again.

battle:sino-japanese:0.text: This is the Second Sino-Japanese War, fought from 1937 to 1945. In red is Japan, an industrial empire that has already taken Korea and Manchuria. In blue is China, poorer and divided, ruled by Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, who have been fighting a civil war against Mao Zedong's Communists. For now, the two Chinese sides agree to fight Japan together.

battle:sino-japanese:1.text: In July 1937, a clash at the Marco Polo Bridge, near Beijing, turns into full-scale war. Japanese armies push south from Beijing. Follow the red arrows. Shanghai falls after three months of fierce fighting, and in December, Japanese troops take the capital, Nanjing.
