There, over several weeks, they carry out the Nanjing Massacre, killing huge numbers of civilians and prisoners of war.

battle:sino-japanese:2.text: China trades land for time. The government retreats far up the Yangtze, to Chongqing, beyond the great gorges, and makes it the wartime capital. Follow the blue arrow inland. Japan holds the coasts, the railways and the great cities, but cannot conquer the vast interior. Its bombers raid Chongqing again and again. In 1941, Japan's war in China leads to an American oil embargo, and then to Pearl Harbor.

battle:sino-japanese:3.text: Now China fights as one of the Allies, with American and British supplies flown over the Himalayas from India. Behind the Japanese lines, Communist guerrillas grow stronger. In August 1945, after the atomic bombs, and a Soviet invasion of Manchuria, Japan surrenders. Somewhere between 15 and 20 million Chinese have died. Within a year, China's civil war begins again.

battle:dunkirk:0.text: This is the evacuation of Dunkirk, from late May to early June 1940. In May, Germany invades France and the Low Countries. Its tanks break through the Ardennes forest, and race to the Channel coast. Follow the red arrow. In blue are the British army and its French allies, now cut off, and pushed back to the port of Dunkirk.

battle:dunkirk:1.text: On the 26th of May, Operation Dynamo begins, an attempt to bring the soldiers home by sea. Destroyers come in under fire, while the soldiers queue on the beaches and the long harbour wall, under attack from German planes. Hundreds of small craft, fishing boats, ferries and pleasure boats, many crewed by civilians, cross the Channel to help. Follow the blue arrow to England.

battle:dunkirk:2.text: By the 4th of June, more than 338,000 Allied soldiers have been carried to safety, many more than anyone had hoped. They leave behind almost all their tanks and guns, and thousands of French troops defending the perimeter are captured. Churchill warns that wars are not won by evacuations. But the core of the British Army is saved, and Britain fights on.

battle:battle-of-britain:0.text: This is the Battle of Britain, fought in the skies over southern England, from July to October 1940. France has fallen, and Britain stands alone. In red is Germany, whose air force, the Luftwaffe, must win control of the skies before an invasion can cross the Channel. In blue is Britain's Royal Air Force, with pilots from across the Commonwealth, and from Poland, Czechoslovakia and beyond.

battle:battle-of-britain:1.text: The Germans attack shipping in the Channel, then the airfields of the RAF. Watch the red arrows across the Channel. British radar stations along the coast give warning of each raid, and Hurricanes and Spitfires rise to meet them. Through August and early September, the RAF comes close to breaking, losing pilots and airfields faster than it can replace them.

battle:battle-of-britain:2.text: Then, in September, Germany turns to bombing London instead, giving the airfields a vital rest. On the 15th of September, huge German raids are beaten off, and soon Hitler postpones his invasion. The bombing of cities, the Blitz, goes on into 1941. But it is Hitler's first major defeat, and Britain stays in the war, later the base for the liberation of Europe.

battle:moscow-1941.text: Autumn, 1941. German scouts come so close to Moscow that they can almost see the Kremlin. Then the mud, the winter, and fresh divisions from Siberia turn the battle. A Soviet counter-attack throws the Germans back a hundred kilometres and more. Hitler's plan for a quick victory over the Soviet Union is over.

battle:pearl-harbor:0.text: This is the attack on Pearl Harbor, on the 7th of December 1941. Japan is at war in China, and has moved into French Indochina. In response, the United States has cut off its oil. Japan plans to seize the oil and rubber of South-East Asia, and first, to knock out the American fleet in the Pacific. Here, Japan is shown in blue, and the United States in red.

battle:pearl-harbor:1.text: A Japanese fleet with six aircraft carriers crosses the North Pacific in secret. Follow the blue arrow. Early on a Sunday morning, more than 350 Japanese planes strike the US Pacific Fleet, at anchor in Pearl Harbor, in two waves. Battleships explode and capsize. The Arizona sinks with more than 1,100 of her crew.

battle:pearl-harbor:2.text: In under two hours, 19 ships are sunk or damaged, and 2,403 Americans are killed. But the American aircraft carriers are away at sea, and survive. The next day, President Roosevelt calls it a date which will live in infamy, and the United States declares war on Japan. Within days, Germany declares war on the United States, and the war becomes truly global.

battle:singapore-1942:0.text: This is the fall of Singapore, in February 1942. Singapore is Britain's great naval base in Asia, called a fortress, and thought impossible to take. In blue is Japan, whose army, under General Tomoyuki Yamashita, has invaded Malaya, to the north. In red is the British Empire, with British, Indian, Australian and Malayan troops, under General Arthur Percival.

battle:singapore-1942:1.text: The Japanese land in Malaya on the 8th of December 1941, the same day as Pearl Harbor, in Asia. Follow the blue arrow south. Moving fast, many on bicycles, they push the British down the peninsula in under two months. Off the coast, Japanese aircraft sink the battleships Prince of Wales and Repulse. On the night of the 8th of February, Japanese troops cross the narrow strait to Singapore island.

battle:singapore-1942:2.text: The island's water supply runs short, and on the 15th of February, Percival surrenders. Some 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops become prisoners, of a smaller Japanese force. Churchill calls it the worst disaster in British military history. Many of the Indian prisoners will later join the Indian National Army, to fight against British rule. The belief that European empires could not be beaten in Asia is broken.

battle:midway:0.text: This is the Battle of Midway, fought in June 1942, in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Six months after Pearl Harbor, Japan's navy is the strongest in the Pacific. In red is a great Japanese fleet under Admiral Yamamoto, with four aircraft carriers. In blue is the United States Navy, with three. The prize is Midway, a tiny atoll about halfway between America and Asia, which Japan means to seize, to draw out the American fleet and destroy it.

battle:midway:1.text: But American code-breakers have learned the plan, and the US carriers lie in wait. Follow the blue arrow from Pearl Harbor. On the morning of the 4th of June, wave after wave of American planes attack, and are shot down. Then, just as the Japanese carriers are refuelling and rearming their planes, American dive-bombers arrive overhead. Within minutes, three carriers are ablaze.

battle:midway:2.text: That afternoon, the fourth Japanese carrier is found, and set ablaze too. The Americans lose one carrier, the Yorktown. Japan has lost four carriers, and many of its best pilots, and its navy will never recover its strength. The fighting moves on to the Solomon Islands, and the initiative in the Pacific passes to the United States.

battle:stalingrad:0.text: Summer, 1942. Hitler's armies push deep into the south of the Soviet Union, toward the oil fields of the Caucasus. In red are Germany and its allies, Romania, Italy and Hungary. In blue is the Soviet Union. The German Sixth Army, under Friedrich Paulus, is sent to take Stalingrad, a great industrial city on the Volga that bears Stalin's own name. Follow the red arrow east across the open steppe.

battle:stalingrad:1.text: In late August, German bombers set the city ablaze. Then the Sixth Army fights its way in. The Soviets, under Vasily Chuikov, cling to a narrow strip along the river, fighting house by house, floor by floor, through factories and cellars. Reinforcements cross the Volga at night, under fire. By November, the Germans hold most of the ruined city, but never all of it.

battle:stalingrad:2.text: On the 19th of November, the Red Army strikes. Watch the blue arrows, one from the north and one from the south, breaking through the Romanian lines and meeting behind the city. The Sixth Army is trapped. Through a bitter winter, the food and ammunition run out, and the cold closes in. On the 2nd of February 1943, the last German troops give in. Nearly two million soldiers were killed, wounded or captured, and from here on, Germany is in retreat in the east.

battle:el-alamein:0.text: This is the Second Battle of El Alamein, fought in the Egyptian desert, in October and November 1942. In red are the German and Italian armies of Erwin Rommel, the Desert Fox, which have driven deep into Egypt, toward the Suez Canal. In blue is the British Eighth Army, with troops from Australia, New Zealand, India, South Africa and beyond, under its new commander, Bernard Montgomery.

battle:el-alamein:1.text: Near the railway halt of El Alamein, the front runs between the sea and the impassable Qattara Depression, so it cannot be outflanked. On the night of the 23rd of October, nearly 900 British guns open fire at once. Then the infantry and engineers clear paths through deep minefields, called the Devil's Gardens, and the tanks push through. For days, the battle grinds on.

battle:el-alamein:2.text: On the 4th of November, Rommel's line breaks, and he retreats, against Hitler's orders to stand fast. Follow the blue arrow west, along the coast. Days later, American and British forces land in Morocco and Algeria, and by May 1943, the Axis armies in Africa surrender. As Churchill later put it, before Alamein we never had a victory, and after Alamein we never had a defeat.

battle:kursk:0.text: This is the Battle of Kursk, fought in July and August 1943, in western Russia. After Stalingrad, the front line bulges far out to the west, around the city of Kursk. In red is Germany, which plans to cut off the bulge with attacks from the north and the south, using its new Tiger and Panther tanks. In blue is the Soviet Union.

battle:kursk:1.text: But Soviet intelligence has learned the plan. For months, the Red Army digs belt after belt of trenches, minefields and anti-tank guns. On the 5th of July, the Germans attack. Watch the red arrows from the north and south. They grind forward only slowly, and on the 12th of July, near the village of Prokhorovka, hundreds of tanks clash in one of the largest tank battles in history.

battle:kursk:2.text: The German offensive stalls, and Hitler calls it off, as the Allies land in Sicily. Then the Soviets counter-attack. Follow the blue arrow south to Kharkov, which they free in August. Kursk is Germany's last great offensive in the east. From now on, the Red Army holds the initiative, all the way to Berlin.

battle:imphal:0.text: These are the battles of Imphal and Kohima, fought in north-east India, from March to July 1944. In red are Japan, which has conquered Burma, and the Indian National Army of Subhas Chandra Bose, which fights alongside it against British rule. In blue are the British Empire and India, with the Fourteenth Army of General William Slim, most of its soldiers Indian.

battle:imphal:1.text: In March 1944, Japanese armies cross the Chindwin River, and march into the hills of Manipur and Nagaland. Follow the red arrows from Burma. They besiege Imphal, and the small garrison at Kohima. At Kohima, the two sides fight at desperately close quarters, at one point across the width of a tennis court. Imphal is supplied by air, while the Japanese, far from their own supplies, begin to starve.

battle:imphal:2.text: In June, the monsoon rains come. The siege of Imphal is broken, and the Japanese army falls back to Burma, shattered, having lost more than half its men, many of them to hunger and disease. It is one of Japan's greatest defeats on land. The threat to India is over, and Slim's army goes on to retake Burma in 1945.

battle:normandy:0.text: This is the Battle of Normandy, which begins on D-Day, the 6th of June 1944. In red is Germany, which has occupied France for four years, and fortified the coast with its Atlantic Wall. In blue are the Allies: the United States, Britain, Canada, and forces from many other countries, gathered in southern England under General Dwight Eisenhower. Stalin has long demanded that they open a second front in the west.

battle:normandy:1.text: On a stormy morning, 156,000 Allied troops land on five beaches, code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, with 7,000 ships and 11,000 planes behind them. Follow the blue arrows across the Channel. Paratroopers have landed in the night. At Omaha Beach, the Americans suffer terrible losses, but by nightfall, all five beaches are taken.

battle:normandy:2.text: The fighting inland, through the high hedgerows of the Norman countryside, is long and hard. In late July, American forces break out to the south, and in August, German armies are trapped and destroyed near Falaise. On the 25th of August, Paris is free. Together with the Soviet advance in the east, the landings doom Nazi Germany.

battle:leyte-gulf.text: October 1944, in the waters around the Philippines. Japan commits almost its entire remaining navy to stop the American landings at Leyte. Over four days, in perhaps the largest sea battle in history, it loses 26 ships. The Imperial Japanese Navy is finished as a fighting force, Japan's oil lifeline from the south is cut, and the first organised kamikaze attacks begin.

battle:bulge:0.text: This is the Battle of the Bulge, fought in the Ardennes forest, in Belgium and Luxembourg, in the winter of 1944. The Allies have freed France, and are nearing Germany's border. In red is Germany, which gathers its last reserves for a surprise attack. In blue are the American and British armies, holding the quiet, thinly defended forest.

battle:bulge:1.text: On the 16th of December, in fog and snow, German tanks burst out of the forest. Watch the red arrow push west. The Germans aim to reach the port of Antwerp, and split the Allied armies. The American line gives way, and a great bulge is driven into it. At the road junction of Bastogne, surrounded American troops refuse to surrender. Their commander answers the German demand with a single word: Nuts.

battle:bulge:2.text: The skies clear, and Allied planes attack the German columns, which are running out of fuel. From the south, General Patton's army breaks through to Bastogne. Follow the blue arrow. By the end of January, the bulge is gone. It is the largest battle the American army fights in the war, and it uses up Germany's last reserves in the west.

battle:berlin-1945:0.text: This is the Battle of Berlin, in April and May 1945. Germany is collapsing. American and British armies are advancing from the west, and the Soviet Union, shown in blue together with Polish forces, is closing in from the east. In red is what is left of Hitler's Germany, defended by old men, boys, and the remains of its armies.

battle:berlin-1945:1.text: On the 16th of April, Soviet armies under Zhukov and Konev attack across the Oder River. Follow the blue arrows. After days of hard fighting on the Seelow Heights, they break through, and by the 25th of April, Berlin is surrounded. The Soviets fight their way into the city, street by street, under constant shelling.

battle:berlin-1945:2.text: On the 30th of April, in his bunker beneath the city, Hitler takes his own life. The same night, Soviet soldiers fight their way into the Reichstag. Berlin surrenders on the 2nd of May, and six days later, Germany surrenders unconditionally. The war in Europe is over. Berlin, divided among the victors, will become the front line of the Cold War.

battle:hiroshima:0.text: This is the story of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, in August 1945. Germany has surrendered, but the war in the Pacific goes on. American bombers have burned many of Japan's cities, and an invasion of Japan's home islands is being planned, at a fearful cost. In blue is the United States. In red is Japan, whose government has not agreed to surrender.

battle:hiroshima:1.text: On the morning of the 6th of August, an American B-29 bomber, flying from the island of Tinian, drops a single atomic bomb on Hiroshima. Follow the blue arrow north from the Mariana Islands. The city is destroyed in an instant. Three days later, on the 9th of August, a second bomb falls on Nagasaki.

battle:hiroshima:2.text: Most of the victims die in moments, others from burns and radiation in the months that follow. Somewhere between 110,000 and 210,000 people are killed. In the same week, the Soviet Union declares war, and invades Manchuria. On the 15th of August, the emperor announces Japan's surrender. The Second World War is over, and the nuclear age has begun. Historians still debate the decision.

battle:chinese-civil-war:0.text: This is the Chinese Civil War. It began in 1927, and its final stage is fought from 1946 to 1949. In blue are the Communists, led by Mao Zedong, strong among the peasants of the countryside. In red are the Nationalists, led by Chiang Kai-shek, who govern China, with American support. Watch the map: the red island off the coast, Taiwan, is where this story ends.

battle:chinese-civil-war:1.text: The two sides first fell out in 1927, when Chiang turned on his Communist allies in Shanghai. In 1934, encircled in the south, the Communists set out on the Long March, a retreat of thousands of kilometres to the north-west. During the war against Japan they fight side by side, uneasily. But when Japan surrenders in 1945, both race to take over the lands it leaves behind.

battle:chinese-civil-war:2.text: In 1946, full-scale war breaks out. The Nationalists have more troops and better weapons, but their government is plagued by corruption and runaway inflation. The Communists win first in Manchuria, in the north-east. Follow the blue arrows south. In the vast Huaihai campaign, in the winter of 1948, whole Nationalist armies are destroyed, or go over to the other side.

battle:chinese-civil-war:3.text: In 1949, the Communists cross the Yangtze, and take Nanjing and Shanghai. On the 1st of October, in Beijing, Mao proclaims the People's Republic of China. Chiang Kai-shek withdraws to Taiwan with his government, and more than a million followers. Millions have died. Taiwan's status remains unresolved to this day.

battle:indo-pak-1947:0.text: This is the first war between India and Pakistan, fought over Kashmir in 1947 and 1948. In August 1947, British India is partitioned into two independent countries, India in blue and Pakistan in red. Hundreds of princely states must choose which to join. Kashmir, a beautiful mountain kingdom, has a Muslim-majority population and a Hindu ruler, Maharaja Hari Singh, and he hesitates.

battle:indo-pak-1947:1.text: In October 1947, armed tribesmen from Pakistan's north-west cross into Kashmir, and advance toward its capital, Srinagar. Follow the red arrow. The Maharaja appeals to India for help, and signs the Instrument of Accession, joining his state to India. Indian troops are flown into Srinagar, just in time to save the city.

battle:indo-pak-1947:2.text: Pakistan's army joins the fighting in 1948. Through the winter and spring, the two sides battle in the mountains and valleys, at heights where few armies have ever fought. Follow the blue arrow north from Delhi. India pushes the attackers back from the Kashmir Valley, but the north and west of the old kingdom stay in Pakistan's hands.

battle:indo-pak-1947:3.text: India takes the dispute to the United Nations, and on the 1st of January 1949, a ceasefire begins. The line where the armies stand becomes the border between the two parts of Kashmir, later called the Line of Control. The promised vote for the people of Kashmir is never held. Kashmir has divided the two neighbours ever since, and they will fight over it again.

battle:arab-israeli-1948:0.text: This is the war of 1948, which Israelis call their War of Independence, and Palestinians remember as the Nakba, the catastrophe. Since the end of the First World War, Britain has ruled Palestine, where Jewish immigrants and the Arab majority both claim the land. In blue is Israel. In red are the Arab states whose armies join the war, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Iraq, alongside Palestinian forces.

battle:arab-israeli-1948:1.text: In 1947, the United Nations votes to divide Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state, with Jerusalem under international rule. Jewish leaders accept the plan, Arab leaders reject it, and fighting breaks out between the two communities. On the 14th of May 1948, as the British leave, David Ben-Gurion declares the State of Israel. The next day, the armies of the neighbouring Arab states invade. Follow the red arrows.

battle:arab-israeli-1948:2.text: The fighting is fiercest around Jerusalem, where Jordan's Arab Legion holds the Old City. Follow the red arrow from Amman. Egyptian forces advance along the coast from the south. After a shaky start, Israel's forces grow stronger and better armed, and in a series of offensives, separated by truces, they take more land than the UN plan had given them.

battle:arab-israeli-1948:3.text: In 1949, armistices are signed with each Arab neighbour. Israel holds about three quarters of the old mandate. Jordan holds the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt the Gaza Strip. Some 700,000 Palestinians have fled or been driven from their homes, and in the years that follow, many Jews leave or are forced out of Arab countries. The ceasefire lines become borders without a peace, and the refugee question remains at the heart of the conflict.

battle:korean-war:0.text: This is the Korean War, fought from 1950 to 1953. Since the end of the Second World War, Korea has been divided at the 38th parallel. In the north, in red, is a communist state under Kim Il-sung, backed by the Soviet Union, and later by China. In the south, in blue, is South Korea, under Syngman Rhee, backed by the United States and the United Nations.

battle:korean-war:1.text: On the 25th of June 1950, North Korean tanks cross the border. Seoul falls within days. Follow the red arrow south. The South Korean army and the first American troops are pushed back into a small corner around the port of Pusan, where they just hold on.

battle:korean-war:2.text: In September, General Douglas MacArthur lands a force behind the North Korean lines, at Incheon, near Seoul. Watch the blue arrow. The northern army collapses, and UN forces drive north, almost to the Chinese border. Then, in late 1950, hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops cross the Yalu River. Follow the red arrow from China. In bitter winter cold, the UN forces are driven back, south of Seoul.

battle:korean-war:3.text: The front settles near the old border, and for two years the armies fight over hills and ridges, while talks drag on. In July 1953, an armistice is signed at Panmunjom. There is no peace treaty, then or since. Between 2.5 and 3 million people have died. Korea remains divided, along one of the most heavily armed borders in the world.

battle:algerian-war:0.text: This is the Algerian War of Independence, fought from 1954 to 1962. France has ruled Algeria since 1830, and treats it as part of France itself. About a million European settlers live there, alongside some nine million Algerian Muslims, who have far fewer rights. In blue is the National Liberation Front, the FLN, fighting for independence. In red is France.

battle:algerian-war:1.text: On the 1st of November 1954, the FLN launches a wave of attacks across Algeria. France answers with force, and sends hundreds of thousands of soldiers. Follow the red arrow across the Mediterranean from Marseille. The war spreads from the mountains into the cities. In 1957, in the Battle of Algiers, French paratroopers break the FLN's network in the capital, using torture on a wide scale.

battle:algerian-war:2.text: It becomes a war of guerrillas, bombs and reprisals, with atrocities on both sides. In France, it causes a deep crisis. In 1958, settlers and army officers in Algiers rise up, and the Fourth Republic falls. Charles de Gaulle returns to power. To the settlers' dismay, he comes to accept that Algeria must be allowed to choose its own future.

battle:algerian-war:3.text: In 1962, after secret talks, the Évian Accords end the war, and in July, Algerians vote overwhelmingly for independence. After 132 years, French rule is over. Hundreds of thousands have died. Almost a million settlers leave for France, and thousands of Algerians who had fought for France face reprisals. The war inspires anti-colonial movements across the world.

battle:dien-bien-phu:0.text: This is the Battle of Dien Bien Phu, fought in 1954, in the hills of north-west Vietnam. For eight years, France has been fighting to keep its colony in Indochina. In blue is the Viet Minh, the Vietnamese independence movement, led by Hồ Chí Minh, with its commander, Võ Nguyên Giáp. In red is France.

battle:dien-bien-phu:1.text: In late 1953, French paratroopers drop into a remote valley near the border with Laos, and build a fortified base, with an airstrip. They hope to lure the Viet Minh into a set-piece battle, and destroy it with their firepower. But Giáp's men haul heavy guns, in pieces, by hand and by bicycle, through the jungle, and up onto the hills that ring the valley. Follow the blue arrow from Hanoi.

battle:dien-bien-phu:2.text: On the 13th of March 1954, the Viet Minh guns open fire, and soon the airstrip is closed. The French can be supplied only by parachute. Strongpoint after strongpoint falls, through 56 days of fighting, in the mud of the monsoon. On the 7th of May, the base is overrun. The next day, peace talks on Indochina open in Geneva, which leave Vietnam divided, and end French rule.

battle:vietnam-war:0.text: This is the Vietnam War, fought from 1955 to 1975. After the French are driven out of Indochina in 1954, Vietnam is divided in two. In blue is North Vietnam, communist, led by Hồ Chí Minh, with the Viet Cong guerrillas in the south. In red are South Vietnam, and its great ally, the United States, which fears that if Vietnam falls to communism, its neighbours will follow.

battle:vietnam-war:1.text: The elections promised to reunite the country are never held. In the south, the Viet Cong rise against the government, supplied by the north along the Ho Chi Minh Trail, through the jungles of Laos and Cambodia. The United States sends advisers, and then, from 1965, combat troops. At the peak, more than 500,000 Americans are in Vietnam, and American planes bomb the north.

battle:vietnam-war:2.text: In January 1968, during the Tet holiday, the communists attack cities across the south at once, even the US embassy in Saigon. They are thrown back with heavy losses, but the shock turns many Americans against the war. Follow the blue arrows south from Hanoi. Protests spread at home, and in 1973, after peace talks in Paris, the last American combat troops leave.

battle:vietnam-war:3.text: Without American support, South Vietnam cannot hold. In the spring of 1975, North Vietnamese armies sweep south, and on the 30th of April, their tanks break through the gates of the presidential palace in Saigon. Between 2 and 3 million people have died. Vietnam is united under communist rule, and Saigon is renamed Ho Chi Minh City. The war changes how Americans see their government, and their wars overseas.

battle:suez:0.text: This is the Suez Crisis, of 1956. The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, and carries much of Europe's oil. It is run by a company owned largely by British and French shareholders. In blue is Egypt, led by its young nationalist president, Gamal Abdel Nasser. In red are Britain and France, the old colonial powers, and Israel.

battle:suez:1.text: In July 1956, after Britain and the United States withdraw their offer to fund the Aswan High Dam, Nasser nationalises the canal company. Britain and France see a threat to their trade, and to their pride. In secret, at a villa near Paris, they agree a plan with Israel. Israel will invade Sinai, and Britain and France will step in, as if to separate the two sides, and seize the canal.

battle:suez:2.text: On the 29th of October, Israeli forces strike into Sinai. Follow the red arrow toward the canal. Britain and France issue an ultimatum, and when Egypt rejects it, their planes bomb Egyptian airfields. In early November, British and French paratroopers and commandos land at Port Said. Follow the red arrow from Cyprus. Egypt blocks the canal, by sinking ships in it.

battle:suez:3.text: The invasion succeeds on the ground, but the world turns against it. The United States, furious at not being told, puts pressure on the British pound, and the Soviet Union makes threats. Britain and France agree to a ceasefire, and their troops leave, replaced by a United Nations force. Israel withdraws from Sinai in March 1957. Anthony Eden resigns, Nasser becomes the hero of the Arab world, and Britain is shown no longer to be the global power it was.

battle:bay-of-pigs.text: April 1961. About 1,400 Cuban exiles, trained and backed by the CIA, land at the Bay of Pigs to overthrow Fidel Castro. The air support they expect never comes, and within three days, Castro's forces have them trapped on the beach. It is a humiliation for President Kennedy, and it pushes Cuba closer to Moscow, towards the missile crisis of 1962.

battle:sino-indian:0.text: This is the Sino-Indian War, fought high in the Himalayas, in October and November 1962. In blue is China. In red is India. The two countries disagree about where their long mountain border lies, at both ends. In the west is Aksai Chin, a high, empty plateau, where China has built a road linking Tibet and Xinjiang. In the east is the land south of the McMahon Line, today India's state of Arunachal Pradesh.

battle:sino-indian:1.text: In 1959, after a rising in Tibet, the Dalai Lama flees to India, and relations sour. India sets up small army posts in the disputed lands, a policy that China sees as a provocation. Talks fail, and through the summer of 1962, patrols clash along the border.

battle:sino-indian:2.text: On the 20th of October 1962, China attacks at both ends of the border at once. Follow the blue arrows. Its troops are well prepared for mountain warfare. India's are not, and many lack proper clothing for the bitter cold. In the east, Chinese forces sweep down past Tawang, almost to the plains of Assam, and in the west, they take the land China claims in Aksai Chin.

battle:sino-indian:3.text: Then, on the 21st of November, China declares a ceasefire, and pulls back in the east, while keeping Aksai Chin. More than 2,000 soldiers have died, most of them Indian. The defeat is a deep shock to India, and it rebuilds its armed forces. The border is still disputed, and the two armies have clashed there as recently as 2020.

battle:six-day-war:0.text: This is the Six-Day War, fought in June 1967. In blue is Israel. In red are its neighbours, Egypt, Jordan and Syria. Tension has been building for months. Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, sends troops into Sinai, asks the UN peacekeepers there to leave, and closes the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. Israel sees the closure as an act of war.

battle:six-day-war:1.text: On the morning of the 5th of June, Israel strikes first. Its planes fly in low over the sea, and destroy most of Egypt's air force on the ground, within hours. Israeli tanks then race across Sinai. Follow the blue arrow toward the Suez Canal. In four days, they reach it.

battle:six-day-war:2.text: Jordan joins the war, and its guns fire on Israeli Jerusalem. Israel answers, and after hard fighting, takes the Old City of Jerusalem, and the West Bank. Follow the blue arrow into the hills. Israeli soldiers reach the Western Wall, holy to Jews, for the first time since 1948.

battle:six-day-war:3.text: In the last two days, Israel storms the Golan Heights, from which Syrian guns had shelled the villages below. By the 10th of June, a ceasefire holds. In six days, Israel has taken Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians are displaced. Sinai will be returned to Egypt after the peace of 1979, but the other lands remain at the heart of the conflict today.

battle:bangladesh-1971:0.text: This is the Bangladesh Liberation War, of 1971. Since 1947, Pakistan has been one country in two parts, separated by more than 1,500 kilometres of India. Power lies in the west, though more people live in the east, in Bengal. In blue are the Bengali freedom fighters, and India. In red is Pakistan's government and army.

battle:bangladesh-1971:1.text: In 1970, the Awami League, led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, wins a majority in Pakistan's elections, but is kept from power. In March 1971, the army launches a brutal crackdown in East Pakistan. Mujib is arrested, and Bangladesh declares its independence. Over the following months, hundreds of thousands are killed, by some counts millions, and around 10 million refugees flee into India.

battle:bangladesh-1971:2.text: Bengali fighters, the Mukti Bahini, wage a guerrilla war, with Indian help. In early December, Pakistan strikes at Indian airfields, and India enters the war in full. Follow the blue arrows: Indian and Bengali forces converge on Dhaka from three sides. In the west, too, the two armies fight along the border.

battle:bangladesh-1971:3.text: On the 16th of December, after just 13 days of full war, Pakistan's commander in the east, General Niazi, surrenders in Dhaka, with some 93,000 men, the largest surrender since the Second World War. Bangladesh is free. In January 1972, Sheikh Mujib comes home to lead it. Today it is one of the most populous countries in the world.

battle:yom-kippur:0.text: This is the Yom Kippur War, of October 1973. In blue is Israel. In red are Egypt and Syria, determined to win back the lands they lost in 1967: Sinai, and the Golan Heights. Since then, Israel has guarded the Suez Canal with a line of forts, and is confident that no attack can succeed.

battle:yom-kippur:1.text: On the 6th of October, Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish year, Egypt and Syria attack together. Watch the red arrow over the canal. Egyptian soldiers cross the Suez Canal in boats, blast through the great sand walls with water cannon, and overrun the Israeli forts. In the north, Syrian tanks push deep into the Golan Heights.

battle:yom-kippur:2.text: Israel calls up its reserves. In the north, it stops the Syrians, and drives them back toward Damascus. In Sinai, Israeli forces under Ariel Sharon find a gap between two Egyptian armies, and cross the canal. Follow the blue arrow to the far bank. They encircle an Egyptian army, while the United States and the Soviet Union rush in weapons to their friends.

battle:yom-kippur:3.text: A ceasefire takes hold on the 25th of October. Thousands have died on each side. Arab oil producers cut supplies to countries that backed Israel, and the price of oil quadruples, shaking the world economy. The war's early successes restore Arab pride, and open the way to talks. In 1978, at Camp David, Egypt and Israel agree a framework for peace, and Sinai is later returned.

battle:soviet-afghan:0.text: This is the Soviet war in Afghanistan, fought from 1979 to 1989. In 1978, a communist government seizes power in Kabul, and its harsh reforms provoke revolt across the countryside. In blue are the mujahideen, the Afghan resistance fighters. In red is the Soviet Union, which sends its army to save the government in Kabul.

battle:soviet-afghan:1.text: In December 1979, Soviet troops cross the border, and fly into Kabul. Follow the red arrow from the north. They kill the Afghan leader, Hafizullah Amin, and install one more to Moscow's liking. They expect to stay a short time, to secure the cities and the roads.

battle:soviet-afghan:2.text: Instead, they stay for ten years. The mujahideen fight from the mountains and valleys, under commanders such as Ahmad Shah Massoud, in the Panjshir Valley. They are armed by the United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, through camps in Pakistan. Follow the blue arrow from the Pakistani border. From 1986, American Stinger missiles let them shoot down Soviet helicopters.

battle:soviet-afghan:3.text: In 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev agrees to leave, and in February 1989, the last Soviet troops cross the bridge back over the Amu Darya. Between 1 and 2 million Afghans have died, and millions more have fled abroad. The war has weakened the Soviet Union, which collapses two years later. In Afghanistan, the fighting goes on, and in the chaos, the Taliban will rise.

battle:iran-iraq:0.text: This is the Iran-Iraq War, fought from 1980 to 1988. In blue is Iran, where an Islamic revolution has just swept away the Shah, and brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power. In red is Iraq, ruled by Saddam Hussein. The two neighbours have long quarrelled over their border, above all the Shatt al-Arab, the great waterway to the Gulf.

battle:iran-iraq:1.text: Saddam sees Iran in turmoil, its army weakened by purges, and in September 1980, he invades. Follow the red arrow across the border. Iraqi forces take the port of Khorramshahr, in Iran's oil-rich south-west, after weeks of street fighting. But Iran does not collapse. Instead, the invasion rallies Iranians around their new government.

battle:iran-iraq:2.text: In 1982, Iran drives the Iraqis back, and retakes Khorramshahr. Follow the blue arrow. Then Iran carries the war into Iraq. For six more years, the war resembles the First World War: trenches, human-wave attacks, and poison gas, which Iraq uses on Iranian soldiers, and on Kurdish civilians at Halabja. Both sides fire missiles at each other's cities, and attack oil tankers in the Gulf.

battle:iran-iraq:3.text: In 1988, exhausted, Iran accepts a United Nations ceasefire. Khomeini likens it to drinking poison. Between half a million and a million people have died, and the border is almost exactly where it was. Iraq is left deep in debt, and two years later, Saddam invades Kuwait.

battle:falklands:0.text: This is the Falklands War, fought in the spring of 1982, in the South Atlantic. The Falkland Islands, some 500 kilometres off the coast of Argentina, have been a British territory since 1833, with fewer than 2,000 people, mostly of British descent. Argentina claims them as Las Malvinas. In blue is Britain. In red is Argentina, ruled at this time by a military government.

battle:falklands:1.text: On the 2nd of April 1982, Argentine forces land on the islands, and the small garrison of Royal Marines surrenders. Follow the red arrow from Buenos Aires. Argentina's military rulers, facing anger at home over a failing economy, expect Britain to accept it. Instead, Margaret Thatcher's government sends a task force, nearly 13,000 kilometres across the ocean.

battle:falklands:2.text: Follow the blue arrows south, by way of Ascension Island. On the 2nd of May, a British submarine sinks the Argentine cruiser General Belgrano, and 323 of her crew are lost. Two days later, an Argentine missile strikes the destroyer HMS Sheffield. On the 21st of May, British troops land at San Carlos Water, while Argentine jets attack the ships in the bay.

battle:falklands:3.text: British troops march and fight their way across the islands, at Goose Green, and in the hills around the capital, Stanley. On the 14th of June, the Argentine garrison surrenders. The war has lasted 74 days, and 649 Argentine and 255 British servicemen have died, along with three islanders. In Argentina, the military government falls, and democracy returns the next year. Both countries still claim the islands.

battle:gulf-war:0.text: This is the Gulf War, of 1990 and 1991. In red is Iraq, under Saddam Hussein, deep in debt after its long war with Iran. In blue is a coalition of more than 30 countries, led by the United States, with Saudi Arabia, Britain, Kuwait and many others. At stake is the small, oil-rich state of Kuwait, at the head of the Gulf.

battle:gulf-war:1.text: On the 2nd of August 1990, Iraqi tanks roll across the border into Kuwait. Follow the red arrow. Within hours, Kuwait City falls, and Saddam declares Kuwait a province of Iraq. The United Nations demands that Iraq leave, and the United States sends troops to protect Saudi Arabia. Over five months, more than half a million coalition soldiers gather in the desert.

battle:gulf-war:2.text: On the 17th of January 1991, the coalition's air war begins. For more than five weeks, aircraft and cruise missiles strike Iraq day and night, and the world watches it live on television. Iraq fires Scud missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia. As they prepare to leave Kuwait, Iraqi troops set hundreds of its oil wells on fire.

battle:gulf-war:3.text: On the 24th of February, the ground war begins. Watch the blue arrows. While some forces strike straight at Kuwait, others sweep far out to the west, through the desert, and around behind the Iraqi army. After 100 hours, Kuwait is free, and a ceasefire is declared. But Saddam Hussein stays in power, and the unfinished quarrel leads to another war, in 2003.

battle:yugoslav-wars:0.text: These are the Yugoslav Wars, fought from 1991 to 2001, as the country of Yugoslavia breaks apart. Yugoslavia is a federation of six republics, home to Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks, Slovenes, Albanians and others. In blue are Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later Kosovo, and NATO. In red is Serbia, under Slobodan Milošević, and the Serb forces it backs.

battle:yugoslav-wars:1.text: In 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declare independence. Slovenia breaks away after a ten-day war. In Croatia, where many Serbs live, war spreads, and the Danube town of Vukovar is besieged and destroyed. Follow the red arrow from Belgrade. In 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina declares independence too, and the worst of the wars begins.

battle:yugoslav-wars:2.text: In Bosnia, Serb forces, backed by Belgrade, seize much of the country, and drive out non-Serbs, in a campaign called ethnic cleansing. Croats and Bosniaks also fight each other for a time. Sarajevo, the capital, is besieged for almost four years, its people shelled, and shot at by snipers. In July 1995, at Srebrenica, Bosnian Serb forces kill about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys.

battle:yugoslav-wars:3.text: In 1995, Croatia retakes most of its land, and NATO bombs Bosnian Serb positions. That November, the Dayton Agreement ends the war in Bosnia. In 1999, NATO bombs Serbia, to stop its campaign against the Albanians of Kosovo. Some 130,000 to 140,000 people have died. Seven states now stand where Yugoslavia was, and international courts have convicted leaders of war crimes, and of genocide at Srebrenica.

battle:second-congo:0.text: This is the Second Congo War, sometimes called Africa's World War. From 1998 to 2003 it is fought across the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a country as large as Western Europe. On one side, in blue, is the Congolese government of Laurent-Désiré Kabila, backed by the armies of Angola, Zimbabwe and Namibia. On the other, in red, are Rwanda and Uganda, and the rebel groups they support. Watch the map: almost all of the fighting happens on Congolese soil, but the armies come from across the continent.

battle:second-congo:1.text: The roots of the war lie in Rwanda. After the genocide of 1994, many of those responsible flee west, across the border into Congo, which was then called Zaire. In 1996, Rwanda and Uganda back a rebellion that sweeps across the country, and puts Laurent-Désiré Kabila in power in Kinshasa. But within two years, Kabila turns on his former allies, and orders their troops to leave. In August 1998, they come back. Follow the red arrows from Rwanda and Uganda into the east of Congo.

battle:second-congo:2.text: Rwandan troops are flown right across the country, to the far west, and push toward the capital, Kinshasa. Angola and Zimbabwe send in their armies to stop them, and Kinshasa holds. Follow the blue arrow up from Angola. The war settles into a long stalemate, with the country split between rival armies and rebel groups. Much of the fighting is over the riches of the east: gold, diamonds, and the coltan used in mobile phones. In January 2001, Laurent-Désiré Kabila is assassinated, and his son, Joseph, takes his place.

battle:second-congo:3.text: Joseph Kabila opens talks. Peace deals are signed in 2002, the foreign armies begin to go home, and in 2003 a transitional government brings the main sides together. The cost is hard to take in. Estimates run as high as five million dead, more than in any war since 1945, and most of them die not in battle, but from hunger and disease. Peace never fully reaches the east, where armed groups still fight today. In the green hills above Lake Kivu, the war's long shadow has not lifted.

battle:kargil:0.text: This is the Kargil War, fought in the summer of 1999, high in the mountains of Ladakh, in Kashmir. In blue is India. In red is Pakistan. Both countries have tested nuclear weapons only the year before. Here, the Line of Control between them runs along ridges more than 5,000 metres high, where every winter, both armies leave their highest posts.

battle:kargil:1.text: In the spring of 1999, as the snows melt, Indian shepherds and patrols discover that the high ridges above Kargil have been occupied. Pakistani soldiers and militants have crossed the Line of Control in secret, and dug in on the heights. Follow the red arrow. From up there, they can shell the only road that links Srinagar to Ladakh.

battle:kargil:2.text: India answers with a huge operation. Its soldiers must climb steep, bare slopes in thin air, often at night, under fire from above. Follow the blue arrow from Srinagar. Indian artillery pounds the peaks, and the air force joins in. In early July, after fierce fighting, Indian troops retake Tiger Hill.

battle:kargil:3.text: Under strong international pressure, above all from the United States, Pakistan agrees to withdraw. By late July the war is over, and the Line of Control is back where it was. More than 500 Indian soldiers have died, and hundreds on the Pakistani side. A few months later, in October, Pakistan's army chief, Pervez Musharraf, seizes power in a coup.

battle:afghanistan-2001:0.text: This is the war in Afghanistan, fought from 2001 to 2021. Blue here marks the Taliban, a hardline Islamist movement that rules most of Afghanistan in 2001. In red are the United States, its NATO allies, and later the Afghan government they support. The Taliban have given shelter to al-Qaeda, the group led by Osama bin Laden.

battle:afghanistan-2001:1.text: On the 11th of September 2001, al-Qaeda attacks New York and Washington, killing nearly 3,000 people. The Taliban refuse to hand over bin Laden. In October, American and British planes begin bombing, while Afghan fighters of the Northern Alliance advance on the ground. Within weeks, Kabul falls, and by December, the Taliban have lost Kandahar, their last stronghold.

battle:afghanistan-2001:2.text: A new Afghan government is formed, and NATO troops arrive to help it. But the Taliban regroup, many of them across the border in Pakistan, and fight a long insurgency, with roadside bombs and attacks in the south and east. Follow the blue arrow. Bin Laden is killed in Pakistan in 2011. At its peak, around that time, there are some 140,000 foreign troops in the country.

battle:afghanistan-2001:3.text: In 2020, the United States agrees with the Taliban to withdraw. In August 2021, as the last foreign troops leave, the Afghan army collapses, and within days the Taliban are back in Kabul. By one major estimate, more than 176,000 people have died directly in the fighting. The Taliban rule Afghanistan again, with severe limits on the rights of women and girls.

battle:iraq-2003:0.text: This is the Iraq War, fought from 2003 to 2011. In blue is a coalition led by the United States and Britain. In red is Iraq, ruled by Saddam Hussein, and later the insurgents who fight on after his fall. The United States and Britain say that Iraq is hiding weapons of mass destruction. No such weapons will be found.

battle:iraq-2003:1.text: On the 20th of March 2003, the invasion begins. Follow the blue arrow north from Kuwait. American and British forces race up the valleys of the Tigris and Euphrates, and within three weeks, Baghdad falls. A statue of Saddam is pulled down in the city's Firdos Square. Saddam is captured in December, hiding in a hole near his home town, Tikrit.

battle:iraq-2003:2.text: But no plan is ready for what follows. The Iraqi army is disbanded, and order breaks down. An insurgency grows, and by 2006, Iraq is in a civil war between Sunni and Shia armed groups, with car bombs and killings every day. In 2007, the United States sends in more troops, and the violence slowly falls.

battle:iraq-2003:3.text: American combat troops leave Iraq at the end of 2011. Hundreds of thousands of Iraqis have died. From the remains of the insurgency, the group called Islamic State will rise, and seize much of Iraq and Syria in 2014. The war reshapes the Middle East, and strengthens the influence of Iran.

battle:syrian-civil-war:0.text: This is the Syrian Civil War, fought from 2011 to 2024. In red is the government of Bashar al-Assad, whose family has ruled Syria since 1971, backed by Russia and Iran. The blue arrows belong to the opposition, a changing mix of rebel groups, in the end led by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham. Many other forces join the fight, among them Kurdish fighters, Turkey, the United States, and the group called Islamic State.

battle:syrian-civil-war:1.text: In March 2011, in the wave of protests known as the Arab Spring, Syrians march for reform. The government answers with force. Soldiers defect, rebel groups take up arms, and by 2012, the country is at war. The fighting reaches the great northern city of Aleppo, which is divided between the two sides for four years.

battle:syrian-civil-war:2.text: The war becomes many wars at once. In 2014, Islamic State seizes much of eastern Syria, and declares Raqqa its capital. In 2015, Russia joins the war with air strikes, and helps the government retake Aleppo in 2016. The government uses barrel bombs and chemical weapons on rebel-held areas. More than half of Syria's people are forced from their homes, millions of them abroad.

battle:syrian-civil-war:3.text: For years the front lines freeze, and the rebels hold only the north-west, around Idlib. Then, in late November 2024, they launch a sudden offensive. Follow the blue arrows: Aleppo falls within days, then Hama and Homs, and on the 8th of December, the rebels enter Damascus. Assad flees to Russia, ending 53 years of rule by his family. More than half a million people have died.

battle:russia-ukraine.text: February 2022. Building on its seizure of Crimea in 2014, Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine holds Kyiv, and wins back ground that year, and the war then becomes a grinding contest of trenches and drones. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers are thought to have been killed or wounded, and millions forced from their homes. Finland and Sweden have joined NATO. This account is as of early 2026.

battle:sudan-2023.text: April 2023. In Sudan, two military rulers who had seized power together turn on each other in the capital, Khartoum. The fighting spreads to Darfur, with mass atrocities reported, and famine declared. According to the United Nations, more than 10 million people have been forced from their homes. This account is as of early 2026.

battle:gaza-2023.text: October 2023. On the 7th, Hamas-led fighters attack southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking some 250 hostages. Israel's air and ground offensive devastates Gaza, where local health officials count more than 60,000 dead. The war draws in Lebanon, Iran and Yemen's Houthis, and is the subject of cases at international courts. A fragile ceasefire began in October 2025. This account is as of early 2026.
